bundles.name: Superpowers
bundles.description: A software development workflow: brainstorm, plan, build test-first, review, then merge.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want the agent to follow a full development process instead of jumping straight to code

glance.label: It does
glance.text: chains its skills into one workflow: brainstorm, plan, build test-first on its own branch, review, then merge

glance.label: You get
glance.text: an approved design, a written plan, tested commits and a review before anything merges

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: by itself: before every reply, the agent checks which of its skills applies

glance.label: Works with
glance.text: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and more, each installed separately

tldr.text: Superpowers makes its skills fire on their own: using-superpowers, loaded at the start of each session, has the agent check for a matching skill before every reply. Building something then follows one path. brainstorming asks what you actually want and ends with a design you approve, in chat for small changes or as a document for projects. using-git-worktrees sets up an isolated branch with a clean test baseline, and writing-plans breaks the design into small tasks, each with exact files, code and checks. The plan runs either through subagent-driven-development, a fresh subagent per task with a review after each, or through executing-plans, inline with one review at the end. Throughout, test-driven-development makes every change start from a failing test, and finishing-a-development-branch verifies the tests, then merges, opens a PR, keeps or discards the branch. Other skills step in when needed: systematic-debugging for bugs, verification-before-completion before claiming anything works, requesting-code-review and receiving-code-review around reviews, dispatching-parallel-agents for independent tasks, and writing-skills for writing new skills test-first.

skills.note: Makes the agent load the other Superpowers skills before it replies; alone, it has nothing to load.
Executes a plan such as writing-plans writes, and has its final reviewer use the prompt that ships with requesting-code-review.
Runs scripts that ship with subagent-driven-development, and loads test-driven-development and verification-before-completion.

bundles.name: Caveman
bundles.description: Terse agent replies, plus compressed commits, reviews and memory files, and lean work patterns.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want shorter agent replies and fewer tokens spent, beyond chat too

glance.label: It does
glance.text: makes the agent answer tersely, and adds terse commits, one-line reviews and compressed memory files

glance.label: Keeps
glance.text: code, commands, errors and numbers exact, and full sentences for warnings and irreversible actions

glance.label: Also has
glance.text: five short work patterns, such as investigate-first and lean-build, that keep code changes small

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: the Caveman plugin for caveman-stats and for cavecrew's subagents

tldr.text: Its core is caveman, a mode that makes the agent lead with the answer in short plain sentences, with no greetings, hedging or recaps, until you say "stop caveman"; ultracave and megacave, two more skills in the repo, cut further. The other skills carry the idea beyond chat. caveman-commit writes Conventional Commits messages with a subject of 50 characters when possible, caveman-review writes one line per review finding, and caveman-compress rewrites a memory file such as CLAUDE.md in caveman style to save input tokens, backing up the original. cavecrew delegates searches, small edits and reviews to three subagents whose reports come back compressed, so the main context lasts longer. caveman-stats shows the session's recorded token usage, and caveman-help lists every mode and command. Five short skills are work patterns the agent picks up when a task fits: investigate-first diagnoses before editing, lean-build builds only what's asked, surgical-patch fixes at the narrowest layer, safe-refactor keeps behavior unchanged and migration keeps changes reversible. The repo also ships a CLI and a proxy that shrink what the agent reads; this bundle covers its skills.

bundles.description: Turns an interview into a file of raw notes, then the notes into an article.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want to write an essay or article from your own ideas, with the agent as interviewer and editor

glance.label: It does
glance.text: first interviews you into a file of raw notes, then turns the notes into an article with you

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a notes file and, in a separate file, an article built one section at a time

glance.label: Then pick
glance.text: writing-beats to choose each next section, or writing-shape to commit to an angle first

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call each skill

tldr.text: Matt Pocock's writing skills split writing into exploring and committing. writing-fragments is the exploring step: the agent interviews you and saves every usable line, anecdote and idea to one Markdown file, with no outline. The committing step takes that file, or any pile of notes, and turns it into an article in a separate file, in one of two ways. writing-beats drafts two or three possible openings, then after each section offers the next possible ones, so you steer the piece one choice at a time. writing-shape has you pick an angle up front, then builds the article block by block, debating with you whether each should be prose, a list, a table or a quote. Both refuse to let a section lean on an idea the reader hasn't met yet. The skills sit in the repo's in-progress folder, so expect them to change.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want the agent to agree with you on what to build before it codes, then build it in small tested steps

glance.label: It does
glance.text: interviews you about a change, writes a spec and tickets on your issue tracker, builds each ticket test-first, then reviews the diff

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a project glossary and decision records, a spec and ordered tickets, tested commits, a review against your standards and the spec, and ideas for next time

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: a code repo, and one run of the setup skill there to record your issue tracker: GitHub, GitLab, local Markdown files or another

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: each main step only when you type it; supporting skills, such as the test-first and review ones, the agent can also start by itself

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: frameworks that own the whole process, each step is a small skill you call yourself and can edit

glance.label: Also covers
glance.text: triaging incoming issues, debugging hard bugs, planning work too big for one session, and finding refactors that simplify a codebase

glance.label: Start with
glance.text: ask-matt, a skill that maps the others and points you to the one that fits

tldr.text: Matt Pocock, a TypeScript teacher, built these skills to keep coding agents aligned with what you want and their code small and tested. A one-time setup skill records which issue tracker the repo uses and what its triage labels are called. The flow then starts with an interview: the agent asks about the change in numbered rounds, each question with its recommended answer, until no decision is left open, and writes the project's terms to a glossary and hard-to-reverse choices to architecture decision records as you go. Questions that talk can't answer go to a throwaway prototype or a background research agent. Next, the conversation becomes a spec on the tracker, then tickets: thin slices that each work end to end and list the tickets that must land first. The build step takes one ticket at a time, test-first, and ends with a review that checks the diff against your coding standards and, separately, against the spec; another skill builds a whole spec at once with parallel subagents. Finally, a retrospective proposes new checks, coding standards or agent instructions so the next run goes better.

bundles.name: RigorPilot
bundles.description: Reproduces a deep learning research repo from its README in small audited steps, with a separate lane for trying new ideas.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want an agent to run a deep learning research repo from its README and record honestly what worked

glance.label: It does
glance.text: finds the smallest documented run, such as one evaluation command, sets it up, runs it and audits the result, instead of a full training run

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a repro_outputs/ folder: a verdict (verified, partial or blocked), the exact commands, logs, patches, and any change to data, evaluation or metrics

glance.label: Main skill
glance.text: ai-research-reproduction runs the steps. It isn't one of the five listed, but the bundle's install command adds it, and two of the five need it

glance.label: Also has
glance.text: ai-research-explore, a separate lane for trying new research ideas, whose results are never reported as reproduced

tldr.text: The repo's main skill, ai-research-reproduction, runs a reproduction end to end. It isn't listed among these five, but the bundle's install command adds it with them. The five are its steps, and each can also be called on its own. repo-intake-and-plan reads the README and project files, sorts the documented commands into inference, evaluation and training, and picks the smallest one worth trusting. paper-context-resolver steps in only when the README leaves out a detail that matters, such as which dataset split to evaluate on, and looks it up in the paper, noting any conflict. env-and-assets-bootstrap drafts conda commands and where checkpoints and datasets should go, before anything runs. minimal-run-and-audit runs the chosen command and writes the evidence to repro_outputs/, including any patch and any change to data, evaluation or metrics; its scripts need the main skill. ai-research-explore, which needs it too, is a separate lane: only when you ask, and starting from a model or run you already have, it ranks and tries new research ideas, writes them to explore_outputs/, and never reports them as reproduced results.

skills.note: Its run and report scripts load a shared runtime that ships inside ai-research-reproduction, the repo's main skill, and stop with an error without it.

bundles.name: BrowserAct
bundles.description: Real-browser automation for agents, plus Skill Forge, which turns a site you scrape often into a reusable skill.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want the agent to use real browsers on logged-in or bot-protected sites, or to turn a repeated scrape into a reusable skill

glance.label: It does
glance.text: browser-act drives your Chrome or BrowserAct's stealth browsers from its CLI; browser-act-skill-forge explores a site once and writes a skill that repeats the extraction

glance.label: You get
glance.text: pages read, clicked through and screenshotted on demand, and tested skill packages (SKILL.md plus Python scripts) for sites you scrape often

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: the browser-act CLI (Python 3.12+, uv). Your own Chrome needs no account; stealth browsers, CAPTCHA solving and browser-act-skill-forge need a free BrowserAct account

glance.label: Asks first
glance.text: before creating or deleting browsers, logging in, submitting forms or uploading files

tldr.text: BrowserAct is a browser-automation service for AI agents, and these skills use its local CLI rather than its cloud product. browser-act lets the agent open pages in your own Chrome, reusing your logins, or in BrowserAct's stealth browsers, which each present their own device fingerprint so sites see separate, ordinary visitors rather than a bot. The agent reads a numbered list of page elements and clicks or types by number, takes screenshots, captures network responses, and can send you a live link to take over when it gets stuck. browser-act-skill-forge builds on browser-act, which it loads first. You describe the data you want from a site and confirm a plan; it works out how the site loads that data, preferring the site's own data APIs over scraping its HTML, then generates a skill of SKILL.md plus Python scripts, has a subagent test it, fixes what fails and installs it. Later runs call that skill without exploring again, which suits bulk jobs such as hundreds of listings. Beyond the free account, only managed proxies and more than five stealth browsers cost money.

skills.note: Loads the browser-act skill in its first step and explores every site through it, so it needs that skill and its CLI installed.

tldr.text: It turns the agent into a scout for the open skills ecosystem. When you ask how to do something, the agent first checks the skills.sh leaderboard for a well-known skill, then searches with npx skills find using specific keywords. Before recommending anything it vets it: the install count, whether the publisher is a known source, and the repo's GitHub stars, with caution under 100 installs or stars. It presents each option with what it does, its numbers, the install command and a link, and can install the one you pick. If nothing fits, it says so, offers to help directly, and suggests writing your own skill with npx skills init.

skills.name: setup-matt-pocock-skills
skills.description: Sets up a repo for the Matt Pocock skills: issue tracker, triage labels and domain docs.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're about to use Matt Pocock's engineering skills in a repo for the first time

glance.label: It does
glance.text: asks where your issues live, which status labels to use and where the glossary and decision records go, then writes it all down

glance.label: You get
glance.text: an "Agent skills" section in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, pointing to config files under docs/agents/

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call it, normally once per repo

tldr.text: The bundle's skills that file specs and tickets, or sort incoming issues, need to know where issues go and where the project's glossary and decision records (ADRs) live; this skill records it for them. The agent first looks around: the git remote, an existing CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, glossary and ADR folders, signs of a monorepo. Then it asks one question at a time, each with a recommended answer you can accept in a word. Where do issues live: GitHub (through the gh CLI), GitLab (through glab), Markdown files under .scratch/ in the repo, or something else you describe, like Jira or Linear? If the bundle's triage skill is installed: keep its five default status labels, such as needs-triage and ready-for-agent, or map them to labels you already use? Only in a monorepo does it offer a separate glossary per part of the codebase. It shows you drafts before writing, edits whichever of CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md already exists, and creates missing labels on GitHub or GitLab. You can edit the files by hand later; rerun it only to switch trackers or start over.

glance.text: maps your situation onto one skill or a path through several, reading each skill before recommending it

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a recommendation of which skills to run, in what order; you run them yourself

glance.label: Also covers
glance.text: between phases of work, whether to keep the session going, clear it, compact it, write a handoff or use a subagent

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call it

tldr.text: A router: it knows how the bundle's skills fit together and points you to the right one. Most work follows one main path from idea to shipped code: an interview that sharpens the idea, an optional throwaway prototype, a spec split into tickets, each ticket built test-first and reviewed, then a retrospective that improves the agent's setup for next time. Other starting points join that path: sorting incoming issues, chasing a hard bug, or planning an effort too big for one session. It also places the standalone skills, such as research, teaching and handoffs, and the setup skill to run first. Between phases it walks a short decision tree: stay in the session if the next phase needs what's in it, clear it if nothing there matters, write a handoff only when the work moves to another tool, folder or person, send self-contained tasks to a subagent, and otherwise compact the conversation.

skills.name: skill-creator
skills.description: Creates, improves and eval-tests skills.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want to write a new skill, or find out whether an existing one actually helps

glance.label: It does
glance.text: drafts the skill with you, runs test prompts with and without it, and lets you review the outputs side by side

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a SKILL.md revised over rounds of tests, with a benchmark of pass rate, time and tokens

glance.label: Also tunes
glance.text: the description agents read to decide whether to load the skill, so it's picked up when it should be and not otherwise

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: simpler skill-writing skills such as write-a-skill, it runs the skill on test prompts and measures the difference

glance.label: Works best in
glance.text: Claude Code; claude.ai skips the comparison runs, the benchmark and description tuning

tldr.text: Anthropic's own skill for making skills. It starts wherever you are: an idea, a workflow you just did in the conversation ("turn this into a skill"), or a draft. It asks what the skill should do, when it should be used and what it should produce, then writes the SKILL.md. Next it writes two or three test prompts and runs each twice in parallel subagents, once with the skill and once without it, or with the old version. While they run it drafts pass-or-fail checks for the outputs, then grades them, totals pass rate, time and tokens into a benchmark, and opens a viewer in your browser where you click through each output and leave comments. It rewrites the skill from your feedback, preferring general fixes over ones tailored to the tests, and repeats until you're happy. Finally it can tune the description: you approve 20 sample requests, some that should load the skill and some that look similar but shouldn't, and a script tries up to five rewrites, keeping the one that scores best on requests it didn't learn from. To compare two versions, it can also have an agent judge their outputs without knowing which is which.

skills.name: writing-great-skills
skills.description: Teaches the vocabulary and principles that make a skill predictable.

skills.name: writing-for-agents
skills.description: Guides writing documents for agents: skills, AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're writing or editing a skill, an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, or any doc an agent reads

glance.label: It does
glance.text: gives the agent principles for writing docs that agents follow the same way every run

glance.label: You get
glance.text: tighter agent docs: sharper descriptions, clear steps, reference moved into separate files, dead lines pruned

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: by itself whenever you create or edit a skill, AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md

tldr.text: Its goal is an agent that takes the same steps every run, even when the output differs. The lines an agent always sees, such as a skill's description or a line in AGENTS.md pointing to a doc, decide when it opens other material, so they should be sharply worded, with one trigger per case, and short, since they cost tokens every turn. Steps stay in the main file; reference that only some cases need moves to separate files. Each step should end on a condition the agent can check, so it doesn't stop early. Familiar words that carry a whole behaviour, like "tight" for a fast, reliable loop, beat spelling it out each time, and saying what to do works better than banning what not to do, since a ban puts the unwanted behaviour in mind. It prunes duplicates, stale lines, facts the agent can look up itself and instructions it would follow anyway. For skills, it also covers frontmatter and the choice between letting the agent start a skill, which costs tokens every turn, and leaving it to you, which means remembering it exists.

skills.name: using-superpowers
skills.description: Makes the agent look for and invoke a matching skill before every response.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you install the Superpowers bundle: it's the bundle's entry point

glance.label: It does
glance.text: makes the agent check for a matching skill before every reply, even before a clarifying question

glance.label: Priority
glance.text: process skills such as brainstorming and systematic-debugging come before implementation skills

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: the rest of Superpowers to be useful

tldr.text: It's the rule that makes the other Superpowers skills fire. Loaded at the start of a session, it tells the agent that if there's even a 1% chance a skill applies, it must load it before responding, including before asking a question or exploring the code, and announce which skill it's using. When several apply, process skills come first: brainstorming before building, systematic-debugging before fixing. It lists the excuses agents use to skip skills and answers each one, adapts to harnesses such as Claude Code and Codex, and gives way to your own instructions in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. Subagents ignore it.

skills.name: write-a-skill
skills.description: Scaffolds a new skill with progressive disclosure and bundled resources.

skills.name: writing-skills
skills.description: Writes skills test-first: pressure-test with subagents, then document.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're writing or editing a skill and want proof that agents actually follow it

glance.label: It does
glance.text: tests a skill like code: run a subagent without it and watch it go wrong, then write the skill and check the subagent now behaves

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a SKILL.md that answers the exact excuses agents gave in testing, with a description that only says when to use it

glance.label: Unlike skill-creator
glance.text: Anthropic's skill-creator scores a skill's outputs on test prompts; this checks whether agents obey it when tempted to cut corners

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: subagents, to run the tests

tldr.text: Its rule is "no skill without a failing test first", for new skills and edits alike. The agent first gives a subagent a task that tempts it to break the rule the skill will teach, such as a scenario with a deadline, hours of work it would have to throw away, and the end of a long day. It runs this without the skill and notes every excuse the subagent gives, word for word. Then it writes the smallest skill that answers those excuses, reruns the tests until the subagent complies, and closes each new loophole it finds. Along the way it teaches how to write skills agents find and follow. The description says only when to use the skill, never its steps, because agents follow a summary instead of reading the body. Skills that load in every session stay under about 200 words. Rules agents skip under pressure get a table of excuses with answers; output that comes out in the wrong form gets a plain description of what to produce instead. Before full tests, new wording is tried on five or more fresh agents and compared with agents given no guidance.

skills.name: browser-act-skill-forge
skills.description: Turns a browser exploration of a website into a reusable skill.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you'll pull data from, or act on, the same website again and again, or need hundreds or thousands of records from it

glance.label: It does
glance.text: explores the site once in your browser, finds the data requests its pages make, or else reads the page, and builds a skill from that

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a tested, installed skill per reusable step, such as search or a detail page: a SKILL.md plus Python scripts

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: the browser-act skill, and an API key from BrowserAct, a browser-automation service with a free tier

glance.label: Unlike browser-act
glance.text: which drives a browser for one task, it keeps what it learned as a skill you can rerun

tldr.text: You say what data you want, or what action to perform, on which site; without a site, it searches for candidates and lets you choose. It splits the job into steps you'd reuse on their own, such as search or reading a detail page, confirms one plan with you, then works without further questions. For each step it explores the site in your logged-in browser, preferring the requests the site's own pages send to its servers over reading the page, and records exactly how to repeat them. It wraps each working piece in a Python script, writes a SKILL.md around it, has a subagent test it, and fixes and retests until it passes before installing it. If you asked for data now, such as 500 listings, it then runs the new skill in batches. It reads only what you could see yourself in that browser, and never uses third-party scrapers or the site's official developer API, so the result needs no extra keys. Recordings and results stay on your machine.

skills.name: skill-vetter
skills.description: Vets a skill for red flags and permission scope before you install it.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're about to install a skill from ClawHub, GitHub or another agent and want to know it's safe

glance.label: It does
glance.text: has the agent read every file of the skill against a list of red flags and rate its risk

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a vetting report: source, red flags, files, network and commands it needs, risk level and a verdict

glance.label: Rejects
glance.text: calls to unknown URLs, credential requests, base64 decoding, eval, obfuscated code, sudo, and reading ~/.ssh or the agent's memory files

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: the SkillScan skill, which runs a Python scanner and blocks risky skills, it's a checklist the agent works through by reading the code

tldr.text: A short security protocol for agents that install skills, aimed at the OpenClaw agent and its ClawHub skill registry. First the agent checks where the skill comes from: the author, downloads or stars, last update. Then it reads all of the skill's files for red flags: calls to unknown URLs or bare IP addresses, sending data out, asking for tokens or API keys, reading ~/.ssh, ~/.aws or the agent's own memory and identity files such as MEMORY.md and SOUL.md, base64 decoding, eval, obfuscated code, sudo, or installing packages it doesn't list. Any one of these means reject. A skill that passes is then weighed by what it reads, writes, runs and connects to, against what it claims to do, and sorted into four risk levels: low, such as notes or formatting (install); medium, such as files, browsers or APIs (full code review); high, such as credentials or trading (your approval); extreme, such as root access (don't install). Official skills and popular repos get a lighter review than unknown authors, but still a review. For skills on GitHub, it gives curl commands that check stars and fetch the files before installing.

skills.name: skillscan
skills.description: Acts as a security gate that every newly installed skill must pass.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you install skills from hubs or repos and want each one checked for malicious code before use

glance.label: It does
glance.text: uploads each new skill to an online scanner run by its maker, TokAuth, and acts on the risk verdict

glance.label: Blocks
glance.text: high and critical risk skills, offering to delete them; low and medium ones need your OK; safe ones, and ones without a verdict, go ahead

glance.label: Sends
glance.text: with each scan, a client ID, your operating system and your machine's MAC address when it can read it

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: by itself whenever a skill is installed, loaded or questioned; on first load it offers to scan every installed skill

glance.label: Updates
glance.text: itself from TokAuth's server once a day, without asking

glance.label: Unlike skill-vetter
glance.text: which has the agent read the skill's code for red flags; here the analysis happens on a remote server

tldr.text: SkillScan sets itself up as a gate: whenever a skill arrives, however it comes (a .zip, a git clone, npx skills add, a skill hub), the agent runs its Python scanner on it. A .zip is scanned before it's installed, anything else right after its files land. The scanner hashes the skill's folder and asks TokAuth's server whether that exact content has been scanned before; if not, it uploads the skill as a zip and waits up to three minutes for the verdict. Skills with no verdict, because the scan came back unknown, are let through like safe ones. It needs Python and network access to skillscan.tokauth.com.

skills.name: grill-me
skills.description: Interviews you relentlessly to sharpen a plan or design.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you have a plan or design you haven't fully thought through

glance.label: It does
glance.text: starts the grilling skill: rounds of numbered questions, each with a recommended answer

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: the grilling skill, from the same bundle

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call it

tldr.text: A shortcut: its whole SKILL.md tells the agent to load the grilling skill, so once started the two behave the same. The difference is how they start. grill-me only runs when you call it by name, while the agent can pick up grilling by itself when you say you want your thinking stress-tested. During the session, the agent maps your plan as a tree of decisions and questions you round by round until nothing is left assumed.

skills.note: Now a one-line alias that calls the grilling skill.

skills.name: grill-with-docs
skills.description: Runs the same interview and writes ADRs and a glossary as it goes.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want a plan or design stress-tested in a repo, with the terms and decisions written down as you go

glance.label: It does
glance.text: questions you in numbered rounds until nothing is left assumed, updating the glossary and decision records as answers settle

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a sharpened plan, plus new entries in GLOSSARY.md and ADRs (short decision records) in the repo

glance.label: Unlike grill-me
glance.text: it leaves a paper trail; grill-me runs the same interview and saves nothing

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call it

tldr.text: It combines two other skills from the same bundle. grilling runs the interview: it works through your plan one open decision at a time, asking numbered questions, each with a recommended answer, until every decision is settled, and it looks up facts in your files itself instead of asking you. domain-modeling runs alongside: it calls out words that clash with GLOSSARY.md or are vague ("account": the customer or the user?), invents edge cases, checks your claims against the code, adds each settled term to GLOSSARY.md right away, and offers an ADR only for a decision that is hard to reverse, surprising, and a real trade-off. It's the usual first step of the bundle's workflow when you're working in a repo.

skills.note: Calls the grilling and domain-modeling skills.

skills.name: handoff
skills.description: Compacts the conversation into a handoff document for another agent.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: the work has to move to another tool, another folder, a colleague or a side session

glance.label: It does
glance.text: summarizes the conversation into one Markdown file a fresh agent can continue from

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a handoff file in your system's temp folder, ending with the skills the next agent should load

glance.label: Unlike claude-handoff
glance.text: which also starts a background Claude Code agent on the summary, this only writes the file; you start the next session

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call it, optionally with what the next session is for

tldr.text: The agent writes up the current conversation so another agent can pick up the work. The file goes to the OS temp folder ($TMPDIR or /tmp, %TEMP% on Windows), not your project. It links to specs, plans, ADRs, issues, commits and diffs by path or URL instead of copying them, strips API keys, passwords and personal information, and lists the skills the next agent should load. If you say what the next session will focus on, the summary is tailored to it. To carry on in the same tool and folder, the bundle suggests compacting the conversation instead.

skills.name: prototype
skills.description: Builds a throwaway prototype to answer a design question.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a design question is hard to settle on paper: does this state model hold up, or what should this screen look like?

glance.label: It does
glance.text: builds throwaway code shaped by the question: a clickable logic demo, or several UI variants to flip between

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a prototype to try; once it has answered, the decision goes into the real code and the prototype onto a side branch

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: by itself when you ask to sanity-check some logic or explore what a UI should look like

tldr.text: It first works out which kind of question it's answering. For logic, it writes one self-contained HTML file anyone can double-click, a non-developer included: the current state shown in plain domain words, a button for each action, and tabs of guided scenarios that walk through the happy path, a tricky edge case and something that should be impossible. The logic sits in a small pure module that can later move into the real code. For UI, it builds three to five structurally different versions, usually inside the existing page, switched with a ?variant= URL parameter and a floating bar that's hidden in production. Either way there are no tests, no saved data and no polish, and the full state is always on screen. Once the question is answered, the winning decision goes into the real code, the prototype is committed to a throwaway branch outside main, and the verdict is noted on the related issue or in a commit, pointing to that branch.

skills.name: grilling
skills.description: Stress-tests a plan, decision or idea, one round of questions at a time.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you have a plan, design or decision you haven't fully thought through

glance.label: It does
glance.text: asks every question it can in numbered rounds, each with its recommended answer

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a shared understanding, with nothing left assumed, before any work starts

glance.label: Also called
glance.text: grill-me, a shortcut you call by name

tldr.text: The agent treats your plan as a tree of decisions, where each decision opens further ones. Each round, it asks every question whose prerequisites are already settled: numbered, each with the answer it recommends, and worded so that "yes" accepts it. Your answers settle those branches and unlock the next round. Facts it can find in your files or tools, it looks up itself, with a subagent if needed, instead of asking you; the decisions stay yours. It ends when every branch has been visited, and doesn't act on the plan until you confirm you're aligned.

skills.name: teach
skills.description: Teaches you a skill or concept across sessions, inside the workspace.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want to learn a topic, code or not, over several sessions rather than get a one-off explanation

glance.label: It does
glance.text: turns the current folder into a course: asks why you're learning, gathers trusted sources and writes short lessons

glance.label: You get
glance.text: HTML lessons and printable reference sheets, plus files tracking your goal, sources and progress, all in the folder

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call it, with what you'd like to learn

tldr.text: The folder holds the state of your learning, so each session picks up where the last one stopped. MISSION.md records why you want to learn the topic, and every lesson ties back to it; if that's unclear, the agent asks you first. RESOURCES.md lists trusted sources, since it's told not to trust its own memory, and lessons cite them. Each lesson is one short, well-designed HTML file that teaches one thing, pitched just beyond what you already know. It judges that from its learning records: one numbered note per insight you've gained, revised as you go. A lesson teaches what you need to know, then makes you practise with quizzes or real-world exercises that give quick feedback, asking you to recall from memory and spreading practice over time so it sticks. Each one recommends a primary source and links to reference sheets: cheat sheets, syntax, glossaries. For questions that need real-world experience, it points you to communities such as forums or local groups. It notes how you like to be taught in NOTES.md.

skills.name: domain-modeling
skills.description: Builds and sharpens the project's domain model, CONTEXT.md and ADRs.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're pinning down what your project's business terms mean, editing its GLOSSARY.md, or recording a design decision

glance.label: It does
glance.text: challenges vague or conflicting terms, tests them with edge cases and checks them against the code

glance.label: You get
glance.text: an up-to-date GLOSSARY.md and, for the big decisions only, ADRs (short decision records) in docs/adr/

glance.label: Unlike grill-with-docs
glance.text: it runs no interview of its own; it steps in whenever terms come up, and grill-with-docs runs it alongside its questions

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: by itself when terminology, the glossary or a decision record comes up

tldr.text: It keeps the project's vocabulary straight: the words people and code use for the things the software deals with, like orders, customers or cancellations. It's for changing that vocabulary, not just looking it up. When you use a word differently from GLOSSARY.md, the agent says so at once; when a word is vague ("account": the customer or the user?), it proposes a precise one. It invents concrete scenarios that force you to say where one concept ends and another begins, and when you describe how something works, it checks the code and flags any contradiction. Each settled term goes into GLOSSARY.md immediately, and the glossary holds definitions only, no implementation details. It offers an ADR only when a decision is hard to reverse, would puzzle a future reader, and came from a real trade-off. Files are created only once there's something to write in them; a large repo can keep one glossary per area.

skills.name: codebase-design
skills.description: Gives a shared vocabulary and principles for designing deep modules.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're designing or reshaping a module's interface, deciding where code can be swapped out, or making it easier to test

glance.label: It does
glance.text: gives the agent fixed terms and rules for deep modules: a lot of behaviour behind an interface that's quick to learn

glance.label: You get
glance.text: design discussions in one shared vocabulary, judged by how much callers get for what they must learn

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: by itself in design talk, or when another skill of the bundle needs the vocabulary

tldr.text: The agent sticks to a small glossary instead of looser words like "component" or "service". A module is anything with an interface, from one function to a whole slice of the app. Its interface is everything a caller must know, including ordering rules, errors and performance, not just the type signature. A module is deep when callers get a lot of behaviour from an interface they can learn quickly, and shallow when the interface is nearly as complex as the code behind it. A seam is a place where behaviour can be swapped without editing the code there, and an adapter is what plugs in, such as a Postgres repository or an in-memory fake. Rules of thumb follow: if deleting a module would spread its complexity across its callers, it was earning its keep; tests go through the same interface callers use; add a seam only once two adapters actually need it. For testability: pass dependencies in, return results instead of changing things on the side. An extra file has several subagents each design a very different interface, to compare before choosing.

skills.name: wayfinder
skills.description: Plans work too big for one session as a map of decision tickets.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: an effort is too big and unclear for one session, like a new project or a huge feature

glance.label: It does
glance.text: lists the open decisions as tickets on your issue tracker, then settles one ticket per session

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a parent issue recording every decision made, ready to turn into a spec: decisions, not code

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: an issue tracker set up by setup-matt-pocock-skills, or it falls back to local Markdown files

glance.label: Unlike grill-with-docs
glance.text: which sharpens an idea in one interview, it spreads the decisions over many sessions

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call it

tldr.text: The first session asks you what the end point is: a spec, a decision, or a change such as a data migration. Then it questions you across the whole effort to find the decisions still open. It creates one parent issue as the map, listing the end point, decisions so far, questions still too vague to ticket, and what's out of scope. Each question sharp enough to state becomes a child ticket, sized for one session, linked by what blocks what, and typed: research (reading docs or APIs, done by subagents right away), prototype (something rough to react to), grilling (an interview with you) or task (manual work a decision waits on). Each later session takes the first unblocked ticket, assigns it to you so parallel sessions skip it, and resolves it, then posts the answer, closes the ticket, adds a line to the map, and turns questions that have become clear into new tickets. When nothing is left to decide, it stops; to-spec, from the same bundle, turns the result into a buildable spec.

skills.name: to-spec
skills.description: Turns the conversation into a spec on the issue tracker.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you've already talked a feature through and want it written up as a spec

glance.label: It does
glance.text: turns the conversation and the code into a spec, without interviewing you, and files it on your issue tracker

glance.label: You get
glance.text: an issue an agent can pick up directly: problem, solution, a long list of user stories, implementation and testing decisions, out of scope

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: an issue tracker set up by setup-matt-pocock-skills

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call it

tldr.text: It writes up what you've already discussed rather than asking more. The agent reads the repo if it hasn't yet, and uses the project's glossary terms and recorded decisions. It checks one thing with you first: where in the code the feature's tests will plug in, preferring existing places and as few of them as possible. The spec then gives an extensive numbered list of user stories ("As a…, I want…, so that…"), the modules and interfaces to build or change, schema and API decisions, and what makes a good test here. It leaves out file paths and code, which go stale, except a snippet from an earlier prototype that pins down a decision better than prose. The issue is labelled ready-for-agent, so it skips triage. It usually follows an interview such as grill-with-docs, and comes before to-tickets, which splits the spec into tickets that agents build one at a time.

skills.name: to-tickets
skills.description: Breaks a plan into tracer-bullet tickets with blocking edges.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you have a plan or spec and want it split into tickets agents can build one at a time

glance.label: It does
glance.text: slices the work into thin end-to-end tickets, each naming the tickets that must finish first, and checks the split with you

glance.label: You get
glance.text: tickets on your tracker linked by "blocked by" relations, or one Markdown file per ticket in the repo

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: an issue tracker set up by setup-matt-pocock-skills

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call it

tldr.text: It usually takes a spec from to-spec, which describes the whole feature, and cuts it into pieces. Each ticket is a tracer bullet: a narrow but complete path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests) that works and can be checked on its own, and fits in one agent session started from scratch. Building one layer at a time is ruled out, and any refactoring that eases the work comes first. A wide refactor, such as renaming a column used everywhere, is split differently: add the new form beside the old, move callers over in batches, then delete the old form, so CI stays green throughout. Before publishing, it shows you the numbered list, with what each ticket delivers and what blocks it, and revises until you approve. Tickets go out blockers first, labelled ready-for-agent, with acceptance criteria and no file paths; on a local tracker they're numbered files under .scratch/. An agent can then take any ticket whose blockers are done.

skills.name: brainstorming
skills.description: Explores what you actually want before any creative work starts.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're about to build or plan something new, in software or not, and haven't spelled out what you want

glance.label: It does
glance.text: asks one open question per message and plays back what it understood, part by part, until the picture is complete

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a description of what to build that you approve: in chat for a small change, a design document for a project

glance.label: Holds off
glance.text: the agent builds nothing, not even scaffolding or installed packages, until you approve that description

glance.label: Unlike grilling
glance.text: Matt Pocock's grilling asks rounds of numbered questions with suggested answers; this one asks you to describe things in your own words

glance.label: Can show
glance.text: mockups, diagrams and clickable prototypes in a browser tab, if you accept its offer

tldr.text: It assumes the agent knows less about what you want than it thinks. If your request already says everything ("make the icon cornflower blue"), it just does it. Otherwise its first message offers to skip the questions and asks about a real moment or a concrete picture. Each message then ends with a single question. It covers goals, non-goals, what would count as failure, things you've seen elsewhere, and which choices of tools you want to make yourself. It can offer to look through your code or the web, or build a throwaway prototype. As each part becomes clear, it describes it back in 200 to 300 words and asks what's wrong. It then sizes the work: a quick task gets done, a small change is described in chat, a project gets a written design document, committed to the repo. Before you see that document, a fresh subagent reviews it as the person who'd build from it, listing what it would still need to know; the agent settles what it can and brings you only the questions that are yours. For software, the next step is writing-plans, which turns the design into an implementation plan.

skills.name: to-prd
skills.description: Turns the conversation into a PRD on the issue tracker.

skills.name: to-issues
skills.description: Breaks a plan into independently grabbable issues.

skills.name: to-questionnaire
skills.description: Turns a decision you can't answer alone into a questionnaire for someone else.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a decision hinges on knowledge someone else has, and you need to get it out of them

glance.label: It does
glance.text: asks you who the recipient is and what you need back, then writes the questions for them

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a Markdown questionnaire in the current folder, to send for written answers or to fill in together in a meeting

glance.label: Unlike grilling
glance.text: that skill questions you about your own plan; this one asks you only about the recipient and what you need

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you invoke it; the agent won't start it on its own

tldr.text: It doesn't question you about the subject, since that's the part you can't answer. It asks two things, each in one go: who the questionnaire is for (their role, what they know, how they relate to you) and which decisions or facts you need back from them. The questions then aim at the gap between the two. It writes to-questionnaire-<topic>.md: the purpose and the decision riding on it, who it's from and to and how the answers will be used, one paragraph of context, a deadline and a note that "I don't know" is a useful answer, then the questions grouped by theme. They come most important first, since a written reply may come only once. Each asks one thing, leaves room for the answer right below, and adds a one-line "why this matters" where it could be misread. It ends with an "anything else?" catch-all, and the agent checks that everything you said you need is covered.

skills.name: loop-me
skills.description: Grills you about the specs of workflows you want to build.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you'd like to hand recurring work or routines to automation, but haven't pinned down how they should run

glance.label: It does
glance.text: questions you round by round, each question with a recommended answer, until every routine is specified

glance.label: You get
glance.text: one Markdown spec per workflow in workflows/, plus NOTES.md on your tools and your words for things

glance.label: Done when
glance.text: an agent could build the workflow without asking you a single question

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you invoke it; it sits in its author's in-progress folder, so expect changes

tldr.text: It calls each recurring pattern in your life a loop, from your week or your morning down to one repeated task, and the spec for running one a workflow. Name a workflow to design, or none and it goes looking, proposing loops you hadn't noticed. If NOTES.md is thin, it first asks about your world: the tools you use, the channels you process and your own terms for them. Then it questions you in rounds, each question with its recommended answer, and creates, edits or deletes files in workflows/ as answers land. It brings a few terms, used only when a workflow needs them: a trigger, what starts each run, either an event such as a new email or a schedule such as every morning; a checkpoint, where you verify or decide, pushed as late as possible so you're asked once, with everything prepared; a brief, the short, decision-ready summary you read there instead of the raw output. Nothing is assumed: a workflow only gets AI, a checkpoint or a schedule if your answers call for one. It writes specs only; building them is another agent's job.

skills.name: claude-handoff
skills.description: Hands the conversation to a fresh Claude Code background agent.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: the current conversation should continue in a fresh agent, starting right away

glance.label: It does
glance.text: summarizes the conversation, then starts a background Claude Code agent with that summary as its prompt

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a new, named agent already working in the same folder, which you manage with claude agents

glance.label: Unlike handoff
glance.text: that skill, by the same author, only writes the summary for you to pass on; this one also launches the next agent

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: Claude Code, whose claude --bg command starts background agents

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you invoke it; it sits in its author's in-progress folder, so expect changes

tldr.text: The agent writes a summary of the conversation to your system's temp folder, then runs claude --bg with a descriptive name and that summary as the prompt. The new agent starts in the current folder and the command returns at once, so your session carries on while the new one works. The summary names the skills the next agent should load, points to specs, plans, issues, commits and diffs by path or URL instead of copying them, and removes API keys, passwords and personal details, since it becomes the new agent's prompt. Say what the next session is for, and it tailors the summary to that.

skills.name: writing-plans
skills.description: Writes an implementation plan from a spec before touching code.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you have a spec or approved design for a multi-step change, before any code is written

glance.label: It does
glance.text: breaks the work into small test-first tasks, each naming its files, function signatures, tests and the commands that prove it

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a plan file in the repo, checked against the spec, plus a recommendation for how to run it

glance.label: Written for
glance.text: whoever implements it, a person or a subagent, assumed never to have seen the codebase or the spec

glance.label: Next
glance.text: subagent-driven-development, a fresh subagent per task, or executing-plans, the agent working through it alone

tldr.text: The plan holds the decisions an implementer couldn't make alone: which files to create or change, the names and types each task shares with others, the exact values from the spec, and the tests that prove each task. Each task is one test cycle: write the failing test, run it and see it fail, write the code, run it and see it pass, commit, with the expected output of every command. The code itself is left to the implementer, except for an algorithm the tests don't pin down. The plan also lists the project-wide constraints and the five likeliest ways real use could break the software that no test covers yet, each then given a test. The agent checks the plan against the spec for gaps, mismatched names and bloat, fixes what it finds, and asks you to review it and choose how it runs: a fresh subagent and review per task, or the agent working through it inline with one review at the end.

skills.name: design-an-interface
skills.description: Generates radically different interface designs for a module with parallel subagents.

skills.name: request-refactor-plan
skills.description: Interviews you into a tiny-commit refactor plan and files it as an issue.

skills.name: ubiquitous-language
skills.description: Extracts a DDD-style glossary from the conversation.

skills.name: improve-codebase-architecture
skills.description: Scans a codebase for deepening opportunities, renders an HTML report, then grills through the one you pick.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a codebase has grown hard to change, test or find your way around, and you want to know where to restructure first

glance.label: It does
glance.text: finds places where thin, tangled modules could become one deep module (lots of behavior behind a small interface), then designs the one you pick with you

glance.label: You get
glance.text: an HTML report of rated candidates with before/after diagrams, then a design worked out question by question

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: three skills by the same author: codebase-design for the design terms, grilling for the questioning, domain-modeling for the glossary and decision records

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you invoke it; the agent won't start it on its own

tldr.text: A deep module hides a lot of behavior behind a small interface; a shallow one has an interface nearly as complex as its code. This skill hunts for chances to deepen, for code that's easier to test and for agents to navigate. Unless you name an area, it starts where git history shows the most change. It reads the project's glossary and its architecture decision records (ADRs), then has a subagent explore and note friction: one idea spread over many small files, functions pulled out only so they can be tested, modules leaking into each other, untested code. For each suspect it asks whether deleting it would concentrate complexity or just move it. The candidates go into an HTML page in your temp folder, which it opens: per candidate, the files, the problem, the fix, the gains for tests, a before/after diagram and how strongly it recommends it, plus a top pick. It proposes no interfaces until you choose. Then it questions you through the design round by round, adds new terms to GLOSSARY.md, and offers to record an ADR when you reject a candidate for a reason future reviews should know.

skills.name: tdd
skills.description: Guides test-first feature and bug work with a red-green-refactor loop.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want a feature or bug fix built test-first, or ask for red-green-refactor or integration tests

glance.label: It does
glance.text: has you agree which public interfaces get tested, then loops: one failing test, then just enough code to pass it

glance.label: You get
glance.text: code built in small slices, with tests that check behavior and survive refactoring

glance.label: Unlike test-driven-development
glance.text: the TDD skill in obra's Superpowers set refactors inside the loop; this one leaves refactoring for a later code review

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: by itself whenever you ask for test-first work

tldr.text: Less a procedure than the rulebook for each red-green cycle: write a failing test (red), then make it pass (green). Before any test, the agent proposes which public interfaces to test at, the places where behavior can be observed without reaching inside, each with a note on what it catches and misses. You confirm them, and no test goes anywhere else. Then it works in vertical slices: one test, then the least code that passes it, then the next, each shaped by what the last one taught. Tests check what the code does through its interface, not how: no mocks of your own modules (only of outside systems such as payment APIs or the clock), no private methods, no checking the database behind the interface's back. It also bans tests that can't fail because they compute the expected value the same way the code does, and writing all the tests before any code. Test names follow the project's glossary if there is one.

skills.name: implement
skills.description: Implements a piece of work from a spec or tickets.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a spec or ticket is ready and you want the agent to build it now, in this session

glance.label: It does
glance.text: builds it test-first, type-checks as it goes, runs the full test suite, then reviews the result

glance.label: You get
glance.text: commits on your current branch, already through a code review

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: two skills by the same author: tdd, its rules for test-first work, and code-review, which checks the diff against the spec and the repo's standards

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you invoke it; the agent won't start it on its own

tldr.text: A short skill that strings two others together. Point it at a spec, a set of tickets or a ticket number; it fetches a ticket from your issue tracker and states its title before starting, and asks if the reference is unclear. It builds with the tdd skill where it can, testing at interfaces agreed with you, runs type checks and single test files as it goes and the full suite once at the end. Then it runs the code-review skill over the work and commits to the current branch. One agent does it all, unlike implement-spec, which hands each ticket of a spec to its own subagent.

skills.name: resolving-merge-conflicts
skills.description: Resolves an in-progress merge or rebase conflict.

skills.name: wizard
skills.description: Generates an interactive bash wizard for steps only a human can do, such as credentials or CI setup.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a setup needs steps only you can do, such as copying API keys from dashboards or adding CI secrets

glance.label: It does
glance.text: writes a bash script that walks you through each step: opens the page, says what to click, saves what you paste

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a script that fills .env and GitHub secrets, with a progress count, confirmations and hidden entry for secrets

glance.label: Doesn't
glance.text: run the script itself, or take over steps the agent could do on its own

tldr.text: Here a wizard is an interactive bash script for a manual procedure that's tedious to do by hand and tedious to explain to an AI again: setting up a service, credentials or CI secrets, finding your way around a third-party dashboard, a one-off migration. The agent first reads the repo (.env.example, README, docker-compose, the secrets your GitHub workflows use) and shows you the stages in order, with the value each produces, for you to adjust. It then spells out each stage's path, such as "Dashboard → Developers → API keys → Reveal → copy", and asks you or checks the docs rather than invent a step it isn't sure of. A bundled template handles the experience: one stage per screen, how many are left, a confirmation before anything irreversible, opening links on any OS, and saving values to .env and GitHub secrets. The agent checks the syntax and reads the script through to confirm every value lands where it should, but doesn't run it, since that needs you. The script is meant for one run and then deleted, unless you want the setup repeatable and commit it.

skills.name: git-guardrails-claude-code
skills.description: Blocks destructive git commands with Claude Code hooks.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: Claude Code runs shell commands for you and you don't want it able to push, or to throw away local work

glance.label: It does
glance.text: installs a hook that stops git push, reset --hard, clean -f, branch -D, checkout . and restore . before they run

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a hook script and a settings entry, for this project or for all your projects

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: Claude Code; the hook script uses jq

glance.label: Keeps working
glance.text: in every later session, until you remove the hook

tldr.text: A one-time setup for a Claude Code hook: a script that runs before each shell command and can block it. The agent asks whether to protect this project (.claude/settings.json) or every project (~/.claude/settings.json), copies the bundled script into the matching hooks folder and registers it, merging it into any settings you already have. From then on, a command matching a blocked pattern, including every kind of git push, is stopped before it runs, and Claude gets a message saying it isn't allowed to run it. The agent offers to add or remove patterns, then tests the script with a sample git push command. The script matches text anywhere in the command, so even a commit message that mentions "git push" gets blocked.

skills.name: setup-pre-commit
skills.description: Sets up Husky pre-commit hooks with lint-staged, type checks and tests.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want every commit in a JavaScript or TypeScript repo formatted, type-checked and tested first

glance.label: It does
glance.text: installs Husky, lint-staged and Prettier, and writes a pre-commit hook that formats staged files, then runs your type check and tests

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a .husky/pre-commit hook, a lint-staged config, a Prettier config if you had none, and a commit adding them

glance.label: Works with
glance.text: npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, whichever lockfile it finds

tldr.text: Husky runs scripts on git events, and lint-staged runs a command on just the files you staged. The agent picks your package manager from the lockfile, installs the three tools as dev dependencies and initializes Husky. The hook it writes formats staged files with Prettier, skipping files Prettier can't read such as images, then runs your typecheck and test scripts over the whole project. If package.json has no typecheck or test script, it leaves that line out and tells you. An existing Prettier config is kept; otherwise it adds one with common defaults. It ends by committing the new files, which runs the new hook once and shows it works.

skills.name: migrate-to-shoehorn
skills.description: Replaces type assertions in tests with shoehorn's type-safe helpers.

skills.name: setup-ts-deep-modules
skills.description: Enforces deep-module boundaries with dependency-cruiser.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want each package in a TypeScript repo used only through its entry files, enforced by a check

glance.label: It does
glance.text: adds dependency-cruiser rules: outside code may import only a package's top-level files, never its subfolders, and imports may not form cycles

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a lint:boundaries check run with your type check, an example package, a README, and a pointer from AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md

glance.label: Proves
glance.text: the rules work, by adding a forbidden import and watching the check fail

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you invoke it; it sits in its author's in-progress folder, so expect changes

tldr.text: A deep module is a lot of behavior behind a small interface, and this skill makes that a rule a tool can enforce. Each folder under src/packages (or packages) is a package: its top-level files, such as index.ts or client.ts, are its public entry points, and everything in a subfolder, by convention lib/ for code and tests/ for tests, is private. dependency-cruiser, a tool that checks imports, then fails when outside code reaches into a subfolder or when imports form a cycle. Tests, even a package's own, must also go through its entry files, like any outside caller. Files inside a package still import each other freely, and several small entry files are preferred to one index that re-exports everything. The agent installs it with your package manager, merges into an existing config rather than overwriting it, adds the check to the command that already runs your type check, and leaves tsconfig alone. It's done only once the check passes, fails on a deliberate bad import, then passes again. It doesn't decide which packages may depend on which; that's left for you.

skills.name: test-driven-development
skills.description: Writes the failing test first, then the code.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: the agent implements any feature, bug fix, refactor or behavior change

glance.label: It does
glance.text: makes it write one failing test, watch it fail, write the least code that passes, then clean up

glance.label: Forbids
glance.text: code without a failing test first: code written before its test is deleted, not kept as a reference

glance.label: Exceptions
glance.text: throwaway prototypes, generated code and config files, each only with your permission

tldr.text: Its one rule is "no production code without a failing test first". Each cycle starts with one small test of real behavior, with a clear name and no mocks unless they can't be avoided. The agent runs it and checks that it fails for the right reason: the feature is missing, not a typo. A test that passes straight away is testing existing behavior and gets fixed. Then it writes the simplest code that passes, with no extra options, and runs the project's whole test suite, not just the new test, reporting any failure it sees, even one it didn't cause. Only when everything passes does it refactor. A bug gets a test that reproduces it before any fix. The skill answers the usual excuses (too simple to test, I'll test after, I already tried it by hand, deleting hours of work is wasteful) and lists the signs that mean: delete the code and start over. A companion guide covers writing tests that fail when the code breaks, and when mocking is safe.

skills.name: executing-plans
skills.description: Executes an implementation plan inline in the current session.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you have a plan from writing-plans and want the cheaper way to run it, or the agent can't start subagents

glance.label: It does
glance.text: works through every task itself, test-first, on its own branch, without stopping to check in between tasks

glance.label: You get
glance.text: tested commits, one fresh review of the whole branch, and a list of every decision it made for you

glance.label: Unlike subagent-driven-development
glance.text: which gives each task a fresh subagent and its own review; here the only review comes at the end

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: sibling skills: it runs scripts from subagent-driven-development and loads test-driven-development and verification-before-completion

tldr.text: The agent reads the plan and its spec once, checks where tasks depend on each other's names and types, then takes the tasks in order. For each one it reads just that task's text, runs every step and compares the output with what the plan expects. When the code is wrong it debugs; when the plan is wrong it decides itself, with the spec as the authority. Each decision, and what it costs if wrong, goes into a progress file that also lets the agent pick up where it was after its context is compacted. It stops to ask only before something irreversible, security-sensitive or outside its branch, such as a merge or a push, or when the plan is too broken to guess. A script marks each task complete only if its tests pass. At the end a reviewer subagent on the strongest available model checks the whole branch, or the agent reviews it itself without subagents. It fixes serious findings in one pass, each with a test that failed first, lists its decisions and the minor issues it left, and hands over to finishing-a-development-branch, which offers to merge or open a PR.

skills.name: verification-before-completion
skills.description: Requires running verification commands before claiming work is done.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: the agent is about to say work is done, fixed or passing, or to commit, open a PR or move on

glance.label: It does
glance.text: makes it run the command that proves the claim, read the full output, and only then report what it shows

glance.label: Forbids
glance.text: "should work now", "looks correct" and an early "Done!" or "Perfect!" without fresh evidence

glance.label: Also covers
glance.text: subagents: when one reports success, the agent checks the actual diff before believing it

tldr.text: Its rule is "no completion claims without fresh verification evidence". Before any claim of success, or even a pleased "Great!", the agent names the command that would prove it, runs it in full, reads the output and exit code, and then states the result with the evidence, or the real status if it falls short. A run from earlier in the session doesn't count. It spells out what each claim needs: zero failures in the test output for "tests pass", a build that exits cleanly for "build succeeds" (a passing linter isn't enough), the original symptom retested for "bug fixed", and a line-by-line check against the plan for "requirements met". A new regression test only counts once it's been seen to fail with the fix undone. It lists the usual excuses (I'm confident, just this once, I'm tired), and tells the agent to treat words like "should" and "probably" as a sign to stop and run the check.

skills.name: subagent-driven-development
skills.description: Executes a plan with one fresh subagent per task and a review after each.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you have a plan with mostly independent tasks and want a review gate on every task

glance.label: It does
glance.text: hands each task to a fresh implementer subagent, then has a reviewer subagent check it against the spec and for quality

glance.label: You get
glance.text: reviewed commits per task, a final review of the whole branch, and a list of every decision made on your behalf

glance.label: Unlike executing-plans
glance.text: where the main agent does every task itself with one review at the end; this costs more but reviews each task before the next

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: an agent that can start subagents; it picks a cheaper model wherever a task allows

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: without pausing between tasks; it stops only for irreversible, security-sensitive or outside-the-branch actions

tldr.text: The main agent stays a coordinator and never writes the code itself. It works on its own branch, reads the plan and spec, and checks the plan for tasks that contradict each other. Each implementer subagent gets only its task's text and the names and types it shares with other tasks; it writes the tests and code, commits and reports. A reviewer subagent then checks the diff, and findings go back for fixes, to a fresh implementer on a stronger model if the first one stays stuck. After five rounds the main agent decides what's left itself. Those decisions and any minor findings go into a progress file that also lets it pick up where it was after its context is compacted. The final review of the whole branch runs on the strongest available model; one subagent fixes its findings, and the agent hands over to finishing-a-development-branch, which offers to merge or open a PR.

skills.name: dispatching-parallel-agents
skills.description: Splits independent tasks across parallel agents.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you have two or more problems that don't share state, such as test failures in unrelated files

glance.label: It does
glance.text: gives each problem its own subagent with a focused, self-contained prompt, and starts them all at once

glance.label: You get
glance.text: one summary per subagent, checked for conflicts and confirmed by a run of the full test suite

glance.label: Not for
glance.text: related failures, exploratory debugging, or subagents that would edit the same files

glance.label: Unlike subagent-driven-development
glance.text: which runs a written plan one task at a time; here there's no plan and the subagents work side by side

tldr.text: When failures have different causes, investigating them one after another wastes time. The agent groups them by what's broken, such as one test file or subsystem each, and writes each subagent a prompt with a single scope, the error messages and test names, limits such as "don't change production code", and what to report back. It starts them all at once. When they return, it reads each summary, checks that no two touched the same code, runs the whole suite, and spot-checks the fixes, since several subagents can repeat the same kind of mistake. The skill walks through a real case: six failures across three files, fixed by three subagents with no conflicts.

skills.name: using-git-worktrees
skills.description: Isolates feature work in a git worktree.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're starting feature work or about to run a plan, and want your current branch left untouched

glance.label: It does
glance.text: sets up a git worktree, a second checkout of the repo on its own branch, after asking you

glance.label: You get
glance.text: that separate checkout, with dependencies installed and the tests passing as a baseline

glance.label: Prefers
glance.text: your coding agent's built-in worktree tool, when it has one, over running git worktree add itself

tldr.text: Work in a worktree can't disturb the branch you're on. The agent first checks whether it's already in one, and if so uses it as is. Otherwise it asks whether you want one, unless your instructions already say. It uses your coding agent's own worktree tool when there is one, since the tool can't track a worktree made by hand. Failing that, it creates one under .worktrees/ at the project root (or worktrees/, or wherever your instructions say), after checking that the folder is git-ignored and committing a .gitignore change if not. If a sandbox blocks it, it says so and works in your current checkout. It then installs dependencies for Node, Rust, Python or Go and runs the tests; if they fail, it reports and asks before going on. Its counterpart, finishing-a-development-branch, merges or opens a PR at the end and removes the worktree.

skills.name: finishing-a-development-branch
skills.description: Verifies tests, then merges, opens a PR or cleans up a finished branch.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: the work on a branch is done and you need to decide how to integrate it

glance.label: It does
glance.text: runs the full test suite, then offers three choices: merge locally, push and open a PR, or keep the branch

glance.label: Waits
glance.text: for your choice: it never merges, pushes or deletes on its own

glance.label: Discards
glance.text: the work only if you ask for that yourself, and only after you type "discard"

glance.label: Cleans up
glance.text: worktrees it created under .worktrees/ or worktrees/, never ones your coding agent created

tldr.text: It's the last step after a plan has been carried out, for instance by executing-plans or subagent-driven-development. If the tests fail, it shows the failures and stops: the choices only come after a passing suite. It confirms which base branch to merge into, since merging into the wrong one is costly to undo. A local merge is followed by a test run on the merged result; if that fails, it stops with the branch and worktree intact. A PR is opened with the hosting service's CLI when there is one, following the repo's PR template, and the worktree is kept for review fixes. On a detached HEAD, merging isn't offered. When git refuses to remove a worktree because of uncommitted files, it shows them and asks whether to commit, move or delete them, never forcing the removal. It won't force-push after a rejected push unless you ask.

skills.name: implement-spec
skills.description: Implements a spec through its tickets, with subagents.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a spec has been split into tickets, and you want all of them built in parallel

glance.label: It does
glance.text: puts a subagent on every ticket that's ready, each in its own git worktree, and merges their work as they finish

glance.label: You get
glance.text: the whole spec on one integration branch, code-reviewed, with the tickets closed or a pull request ready for review

glance.label: Unlike implement
glance.text: that skill has one agent build one piece in your session; this runs many agents over every ticket of a spec

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: subagents, and an issue tracker configured with setup-matt-pocock-skills, the author's one-time repo setup

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you invoke it; the agent won't start it on its own

tldr.text: It starts from a spec and its tickets, such as the same author's to-spec and to-tickets skills write. It reads the tickets as a graph: a ticket can start once the tickets blocking it are done, so at any moment some set of them is ready. An optional exploration subagent first saves notes outside the repo for the others to read. Then it creates an integration branch, the one branch everything merges into. Each ready ticket gets a subagent in the background, in its own worktree and branch, building test-first. When one finishes, another subagent merges its work into the integration branch, and any tickets that unblocks are started. Messages between agents stay short and point to the spec, tickets, notes and commits instead of repeating them.
