Once every ticket is done, the branch gets a code review and one subagent fixes everything it raises. It ends by marking the draft pull request ready, if there is one, or closing the tickets the way your tracker does, then removes the worktrees.

skills.name: typescript-advanced-types
skills.description: Teaches TypeScript generics, conditional, mapped and template-literal types.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're writing complex TypeScript types: reusable generic helpers, type-safe API clients, typed config, forms or state

glance.label: It does
glance.text: gives the agent a reference of generics, conditional, mapped and template-literal types, with short examples

glance.label: You get
glance.text: types written along its patterns and best practices; it adds no steps or files of its own

glance.label: Also covers
glance.text: built-in utility types, testing types, common pitfalls and keeping the compiler fast

tldr.text: It's a reference, not a workflow. Each core feature gets its purpose and a few examples: generics with constraints, conditional types (including extracting a function's return type and distributing over unions), mapped types that rename or filter keys, template literal types that build string types such as dotted config paths, and built-in utilities like Partial, Pick, Omit and Record. A separate file holds worked patterns: a type-safe event emitter, API client and builder, deep readonly and partial types, form validation, discriminated unions, plus the infer keyword, type guards and assertion functions. Its best practices include unknown over any, interface for object shapes and type for unions, type guards over type assertions, and strict mode; it also shows how to write tests that check types at compile time. It lists common pitfalls and warns that deeply nested or recursive types slow the compiler.

skills.name: turborepo
skills.description: Guides Turborepo pipelines, caching and filters.

skills.name: ponytail
skills.description: Forces the laziest solution that works: the best code is the code you never write.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: the agent over-engineers: abstractions, options, dependencies or code nobody asked for

glance.label: It does
glance.text: makes the agent take the smallest change that fully solves the task, reusing what the codebase already has

glance.label: You get
glance.text: short diffs, and replies that end with what it skipped or didn't check, and any risk

glance.label: Levels
glance.text: lite only suggests the smaller option, full applies the rules, ultra also questions any part of the request the need doesn't justify

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: for the whole session, until you say "stop ponytail" or "normal mode"

glance.label: Never cuts
glance.text: validation of untrusted input, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, or anything you asked for

tldr.text: It casts the agent as a lazy senior developer: the best code is the code never written. Before writing, the agent reads the code the task touches and lists every place the change must reach, such as callers, tests, fixtures and config. Then it takes the first option that fully works: skip what wasn't asked for and say so, reuse something already in the codebase, then the standard library, then an installed dependency, never a new dependency for a few lines, and only then write the minimum new code. It's lazy about the solution, not the finish: it still updates every caller and test the change breaks, fixes a bug once at its root, adds one small test for non-trivial logic, and leaves a comment on any known shortcut, naming its limit and when to replace it. Where caveman, a skill for terse replies, trims the agent's words, ponytail trims its code.

skills.name: safe-refactor
skills.description: Restructures code while preserving behavior, with verification around each edit.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're restructuring code, by extracting, merging or moving it, and its behavior must stay exactly the same

glance.label: It does
glance.text: sets up a check of current behavior before editing, keeps feature changes out, and moves one piece of responsibility at a time

glance.label: You get
glance.text: restructured code that passes the same checks as before, with every intermediate step still building

glance.label: Unlike migration
glance.text: which moves data, schemas or APIs with a rollback plan, this changes only how the code is organized

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: on its own, whenever the agent sees a task that fits; it's a short list of rules, not a step-by-step guide

tldr.text: Before any structural edit, the agent defines which behavior must be preserved and how it will verify that. It keeps new features out of the refactor, moves responsibility from one part of the code to another one step at a time, and preserves public interfaces, error behavior, ordering and compatibility unless you've said otherwise. Every intermediate state must still build and pass tests, and it adds no dependency or configuration unless correctness needs it. At the end it runs the same verification again, and stops once behavior matches and the requested structure is in place.

skills.name: surgical-patch
skills.description: Fixes bugs at the narrowest layer that owns the wrong behavior.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're fixing a bug or making a small behavior change, and nothing else in the code should move

glance.label: It does
glance.text: reproduces the failure when that's cheap, traces it to its cause, and changes only the smallest part of the code responsible

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a minimal fix with a regression test, and no cleanup, renaming or new abstractions

glance.label: Unlike investigate-first
glance.text: which stops at a diagnosis, this makes the fix and proves it

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: on its own, whenever the agent sees a task that fits; it's a short list of rules, not a step-by-step guide

tldr.text: The agent reproduces the failure first if that's cheap, otherwise gathers the strongest evidence it can. It traces the symptom to what actually causes it and fixes the code there, as narrowly as possible, rather than patching wherever the symptom shows up. It leaves unrelated behavior and your own edits alone, skips any cleanup, renaming or abstraction beyond the fix, and adds only the regression test the task needs. It then runs that test plus the nearest wider check the change affects, and stops once the failure is fixed and the test passes.

skills.name: lean-build
skills.description: Builds features with strict scope to avoid overbuilding.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're adding a feature or an integration and want it complete, but no bigger than what was asked

glance.label: It does
glance.text: writes down what must work and what's out of scope, reuses the existing code, and leaves out options, config and polish nobody asked for

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a narrow feature working end to end, tested against what was asked, plus a note of any omission that matters

glance.label: Unlike surgical-patch
glance.text: which corrects existing behavior in one place, this adds new behavior through all the code involved

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: on its own, whenever the agent sees a task that fits; it's a short list of rules, not a step-by-step guide

tldr.text: The agent derives acceptance criteria and explicit non-goals from your request and the repository. It follows the feature from where it starts through every part of the code involved and builds one complete path, rather than cramming it into one file or a local patch. It hooks into existing code where that fits, and refactors only when patching would duplicate behavior or blur which code is responsible for what. Extra modes, options, configuration and polish stay out unless the criteria need them, and any new dependency, service or migration needs a stated reason. It runs the new path, runs a focused test, and stops as soon as the criteria pass.

skills.name: migration
skills.description: Implements reversible migrations of schemas, data, APIs and dependencies.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're changing a database schema, data format, API, protocol, config or dependency that other code relies on

glance.label: It does
glance.text: maps who reads and writes the current form, then plans both a forward path and a rollback before editing

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a migration done in stages, with old and new versions able to run side by side and each stage verified

glance.label: Won't
glance.text: delete old data or remove the old path unless you separately ask for that step

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: on its own, whenever the agent sees a task that fits; it's a short list of rules, not a step-by-step guide

tldr.text: Before editing, the agent maps the current readers, writers and data shape, how long old and new versions must coexist, and who owns each part. It defines a forward path and a rollback path, keeps existing data intact, and makes any destructive step explicit and separately authorized. If old and new versions may run at the same time during a rollout, both must keep working. It follows the expand, migrate, verify, contract order: add the new form next to the old one, move over, check, and only then remove the old. Retries must be idempotent, and partial failures visible. It verifies the old and new paths at each stage and stops at the stage you asked for: if you asked only to add the new form, removing the old one is a separate request.

skills.name: triage
skills.description: Moves issues and external PRs through a triage state machine and writes agent-ready briefs.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: issues and outside pull requests pile up on your tracker and you want help sorting them

glance.label: It does
glance.text: gives each item two labels, a category (bug or enhancement) and a state such as needs-info, ready-for-agent or wontfix, and moves it along

glance.label: You get
glance.text: labels, comments and closed issues on your tracker, plus briefs specific enough for an agent to build from without you

glance.label: Checks
glance.text: whether a request is already built or was rejected before, and reproduces a bug before going further

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: an issue tracker and labels configured with setup-matt-pocock-skills, the author's one-time repo setup

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you invoke it; it recommends, then waits for your decision

tldr.text: You call /triage and say what you want in plain words: what needs my attention, look at #42, move #42 to ready-for-agent. For an overview it lists untriaged items, items under evaluation, and items whose reporter replied since the last triage notes. For one issue or outside pull request, it reads everything, searches the code for an existing implementation and the repo's .out-of-scope/ folder, where past rejections are written up, then recommends a category and state and waits for you. Before going further it checks the claim: it reproduces the bug, or runs the pull request's code. If the request is vague, it questions you round by round until it's clear. Then it acts on the state: ready-for-agent gets an agent brief, a comment with current and desired behavior, the interfaces to change and testable acceptance criteria, free of file paths so it stays valid as code moves; needs-info gets notes on what's settled and specific questions for the reporter; a rejected feature is written up in .out-of-scope/ so it isn't argued again. Every comment it posts opens with a note that AI wrote it.

skills.name: diagnosing-bugs
skills.description: Runs a diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a bug is hard to pin down, or something got slower, and guessing at fixes isn't working

glance.label: It does
glance.text: first builds one fast command that fails on this exact bug, and forms no theory until that command exists

glance.label: Phases
glance.text: build that command, shrink the repro, rank guesses, test one variable at a time, fix with a test, clean up

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a fix with a regression test, debug logs removed, and the confirmed cause written in the commit message

tldr.text: Its premise is that a hard bug gets easy once you have a feedback loop: one command that fails on this exact bug and passes once it's fixed. So the agent puts most of its effort there, trying a failing test, a curl script, a headless browser, a replayed request, a fuzz loop or a git bisect script, then making it faster and deterministic. When only a person can trigger the bug, a bundled script walks you through the clicks and records what you saw. If no loop can be built, it stops and asks you for access or a captured log. Next it shrinks the repro to the smallest case that still fails, shows you three to five ranked guesses at the cause, each with a prediction that could prove it wrong, and tests them one variable at a time, using debug logs with a unique tag so they're easy to remove, or measurements for slowdowns. The regression test comes before the fix, but only where a test can reproduce the real pattern; if none can, that's reported as a finding. Secrets are redacted from anything it shows.

skills.name: code-review
skills.description: Reviews changes since a fixed point against the repo's standards and the spec.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want a branch, PR or work in progress reviewed: everything since a commit, branch or tag you name

glance.label: It does
glance.text: runs two reviews in parallel subagents: one against the repo's coding standards, one against the issue or spec

glance.label: You get
glance.text: two separate reports, Standards and Spec, and a line naming the worst issue in each

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: subagents; for specs kept in issues, the issue-tracker setup that comes with this skill set

tldr.text: It reviews the diff between the point you name and HEAD. First it finds the spec: an issue referenced in the commits, a path you give, or a matching file under docs/ or specs/; if there is none, the spec review is skipped. It gathers every file that documents how code should be written, such as CODING_STANDARDS.md or CONTRIBUTING.md, and adds twelve code smells from Martin Fowler's book Refactoring, such as a method that uses another object's data more than its own, or abstractions added for needs nobody has. The repo's own rules override these. Two subagents then work in parallel. The Standards one cites each broken rule and flags smells as judgement calls, not violations. The Spec one lists what's missing, what was added without being asked, and what looks implemented wrongly, quoting the spec. The two reports are kept apart and never re-ranked, because code can follow every rule and still build the wrong thing, or the reverse. It only reports; it doesn't change the code.

skills.name: caveman-review
skills.description: Writes terse code review comments, one line per finding.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want code review comments short enough to paste straight into a pull request

glance.label: It does
glance.text: writes one line per finding: the line number, the problem and a concrete fix, optionally tagged as a bug, risk, nit or question

glance.label: You get
glance.text: comments ready to paste, like "L42: 🔴 bug: user can be null after .find(). Add guard before .email."

glance.label: Switches to prose
glance.text: for security findings, design disagreements and authors new to the code who need the why

glance.label: Won't
glance.text: write the fix, approve the pull request or run linters

tldr.text: Caveman is a skill set whose main mode makes the agent reply in short, plain fragments to save tokens. That mode keeps anything saved outside the chat, PR comments included, in normal prose; this skill makes review comments terse too. Each finding is one line, L<line>: <problem>. <fix>., with the file name added on diffs that span several files, and an optional severity: 🔴 bug for broken behavior, 🟡 risk for fragile code such as a race or a swallowed error, 🔵 nit for style the author can ignore, ❓ q for a genuine question. It drops openers like "I noticed that", hedging, praise on every comment and descriptions of what the line already does. It keeps exact line numbers, function and variable names in backticks, and a concrete fix rather than "consider refactoring". Security issues, architectural disagreements and reviews for newcomers get a normal paragraph, then the terse lines resume. It stays in this style until you say "stop caveman-review" or "normal mode".

skills.name: systematic-debugging
skills.description: Finds the root cause before proposing any fix.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a bug, failing test or odd behavior shows up, especially when a quick fix is tempting

glance.label: It does
glance.text: forbids any fix until the root cause is found, through four phases in order

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a fix for the cause, backed by a failing test that now passes

glance.label: Stops
glance.text: guess-and-retry loops: after three failed fixes, it questions the design with you

tldr.text: Its rule is "no fixes without root cause investigation first". The agent works through four phases in order. First it investigates: it reads the error in full, reproduces it, checks recent changes and, in a system with several parts, logs what enters and leaves each one to find where it breaks. Then it compares the broken code with similar code that works, forms one hypothesis and tests it with the smallest possible change. Only then does it fix: it writes a failing test, makes one change and verifies it. If three fixes have failed, it stops and discusses the architecture with you instead of trying a fourth.

skills.name: diagnose
skills.description: Reproduces, minimises, hypothesises, instruments, fixes and regression-tests a bug.

skills.name: requesting-code-review
skills.description: Sends finished work to a reviewer subagent before merging.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a task or feature is done, before merging, or when you're stuck and want fresh eyes

glance.label: It does
glance.text: sends a reviewer subagent the commit range and the plan, with none of the session's history

glance.label: You get
glance.text: strengths, issues graded Critical, Important or Minor with file and line, and a verdict on whether it's ready to merge

glance.label: Then
glance.text: the agent fixes Critical issues at once and Important ones before going on, notes Minor ones, and argues back with code or tests when the reviewer is wrong

glance.label: Unlike receiving-code-review
glance.text: which covers how to act on feedback you've been given; this one asks for the review

tldr.text: The agent fills the reviewer prompt that ships with the skill with what was built, what it was meant to do, and the first and last commits of the work, then starts a subagent with it. The reviewer reads the diff without changing the checkout or starting reviewers of its own. It checks that the code matches the plan, then its quality, architecture, tests and readiness for production. Where the spec says nothing, it judges by what a reasonable user would expect. It also names anything it decided was out of scope, so the agent can rule on it rather than lose it. subagent-driven-development and executing-plans use the same reviewer prompt for their final review of the whole branch.

skills.name: qa
skills.description: Runs a conversational QA session and files GitHub issues.

skills.name: receiving-code-review
skills.description: Evaluates review feedback technically before implementing it.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you get review feedback, from a person or a reviewer agent, especially if it seems unclear or wrong

glance.label: It does
glance.text: makes the agent check each suggestion against the code before changing anything, and push back with reasons when it's wrong

glance.label: Forbids
glance.text: "You're absolutely right!", "Great point!" and any thanks: it states the fix, or just makes it

glance.label: Asks first
glance.text: about every unclear item before implementing any of them, since items may be related

tldr.text: Its stance is technical correctness over social comfort. The agent reads all the feedback, restates each point in its own words or asks about it, checks it against the code, and decides whether it's right for this codebase. Feedback from you, the user, is trusted once understood. An outside reviewer's is checked: does it break something, is there a reason for the current code, does the reviewer have the full context? When a reviewer asks for a fuller implementation of something, it checks whether anything uses it and suggests removing it if nothing does. Once every item is clear, fixes go in one at a time, blocking issues first, each tested. If a suggestion conflicts with decisions you made, it stops and asks you. When its pushback turns out wrong, it says so in a sentence and moves on. On GitHub, it answers inline comments in their own thread.

skills.name: webapp-testing
skills.description: Tests local web apps with Playwright scripts.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you need to check a web app running on your machine: click through it, take screenshots, read console logs

glance.label: It does
glance.text: writes Python Playwright scripts against your app, starting your dev servers first and stopping them after

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a script you can rerun, and the screenshots, page content or logs it captures

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: Python with Playwright, which runs a headless Chromium

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: browser CLIs such as agent-browser or playwright-cli, which the agent drives one command at a time; here it writes and runs whole scripts

tldr.text: Anthropic's toolkit for testing web apps you're building. The agent writes short Python scripts with Playwright and runs them in headless Chromium. A bundled helper starts one or more servers, say a backend and a frontend, waits until their ports answer, runs the script, then shuts them down. The skill gives the agent a decision path. For a static HTML file it reads the selectors straight from the file. For a live app it first loads the page and waits for network activity to settle, then takes a screenshot or reads the rendered page to find selectors, and only then clicks and types. Examples cover finding buttons, links and inputs, automating local HTML files, and capturing console logs.

skills.name: retro
skills.description: Runs a retrospective on a coding session and improves the agent's setup.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a coding session went badly or slowly and you want the next one to go better

glance.label: It does
glance.text: reads that session's logs and looks for fixes to the agent's setup, not to the code it wrote

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a list of suggested changes, most severe first, such as a lint check to add or a rule to move out of AGENTS.md

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: writing-for-agents, a sibling skill on writing docs for agents

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you call it

tldr.text: A retrospective on how the agent worked, aimed at its environment: the repo's files, checks and tools. It reads the session you name, from session logs on your machine, or the current one by default, and looks for seven kinds of improvement: files that were hard to find, mistakes an automated check could have caught, mistakes the review agent should have caught, an oversized AGENTS.md, expensive tool calls, instructions that don't change the agent's behavior, and information the agent couldn't reach, such as dev server logs. It favors deterministic checks: a mechanical mistake gets a lint rule, a pre-commit hook or a CI job rather than a written rule, and a repo with no lint, type check or tests run by a hook or CI is flagged on its own. Judgement calls go in a CODING_STANDARDS.md that the reviewer reads, and AGENTS.md is kept to short pointers to other files. It stops at suggestions; making the changes is up to you.

skills.name: playwright-best-practices
skills.description: Guides writing Playwright tests, fixing flaky ones and running them in CI.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're writing Playwright tests, debugging failing or flaky ones, or setting them up in CI

glance.label: It does
glance.text: points the agent to the one or two guides that fit the task, out of 57, instead of loading them all

glance.label: Covers
glance.text: end-to-end, component, API, visual, accessibility and security tests, plus Electron apps and browser extensions

glance.label: You get
glance.text: TypeScript tests that follow its patterns and are run until they pass, with important ones repeated five times to catch flakiness

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: Anthropic's webapp-testing, which drives a local app with quick Python scripts, it's about building and keeping a test suite healthy

tldr.text: A guide to Playwright testing in TypeScript. The SKILL.md itself is an index: what you're doing, such as writing a test, chasing a timeout, mocking an OAuth popup or splitting tests across CI machines, points to a few of 57 reference files. They cover the basics, debugging, test types, browser APIs, advanced patterns, test architecture, frameworks (React, Angular, Vue, Next.js) and CI. The references hold the substance: find elements by role or label rather than CSS, rely on assertions that retry instead of fixed waits, sort flaky tests by cause (timing, the CI environment, shared data between parallel workers, state leaking between tests) and confirm them with repeated runs, choose between page objects and fixtures, and fake dates, networks, payments or email. After writing or changing tests, the agent runs them, reads the trace when one fails, fixes it and reruns, and moves on only when everything passes.

skills.name: review-loop
skills.description: Revises work until a critic subagent scores it above a quality gate.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: quality matters more than speed: a feature, a spec, a design doc, or code that must be robust

glance.label: It does
glance.text: does the work, has a fresh critic subagent score it from 1 to 10 with specific fixes, then revises and asks again

glance.label: You get
glance.text: the revised work plus a log of each round's score and feedback

glance.label: Defaults
glance.text: at least 2 and at most 4 rounds, stopping once the score reaches 8/10; change them in your request, like "quality gate 9, max 5 loops"

glance.label: Unlike a single review
glance.text: such as one reviewer pass before a merge, it keeps revising until the score is reached, and works on specs and writing too

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: subagents; without them, you paste the work into a fresh chat to get the score

tldr.text: The agent does the task, or reads work that already exists, then spawns a separate reviewer subagent that sees only the work, not the agent's reasoning, so it isn't swayed by what the agent meant to do. The reviewer gets criteria for this task, such as correct status codes for an API or measurable success metrics for a design doc, and replies with a score and issues, each explained, with file and line references. The agent fixes the critical and important ones, reports the round's score, and sends the work back with the earlier feedback, since the reviewer has no memory. It stops when the score reaches the gate after the minimum rounds, or at the maximum, then does a final polish. The reviewer model must be at least as capable as the worker; if scores stall for two rounds on the same feedback, it suggests a stronger model, a lower gate or smaller tasks. It never reviews its own work, inflates the score or runs past the maximum without asking. Each round costs one reviewer call.

skills.name: investigate-first
skills.description: Diagnoses ambiguous failures before editing.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: something fails and the cause is unclear: an intermittent bug, an odd behavior or a performance regression

glance.label: It does
glance.text: separates what was observed from what's guessed, and weighs each explanation by its evidence and by how cheap it is to test

glance.label: You get
glance.text: the cause and the evidence for it, or the exact blocker, with no code changed unless the task asks for a fix

glance.label: Unlike surgical-patch
glance.text: which goes on to fix the bug, this stops at the diagnosis

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: on its own, whenever the agent sees a task that fits; it's a short list of rules, not a step-by-step guide

tldr.text: The agent touches no product code until the problem is understood. It keeps the observed symptom apart from the cause it suspects, and traces inputs, state changes, which part of the code is responsible for what, and the failure output. It ranks its hypotheses by the evidence for them and by how cheaply each could be ruled out, and won't edit anything until one explanation accounts for all the evidence. It stops exploring once it can name the cause or the exact thing blocking it, and reports the cause with its proof.

skills.name: momentic-test
skills.description: Creates and maintains Momentic browser end-to-end tests.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: your project tests its web app with Momentic and you want the agent to write, run or fix those tests

glance.label: It does
glance.text: edits the test YAML for known changes, or steps through the live app over Momentic's MCP tools when the UI is unfamiliar

glance.label: You get
glance.text: new or updated .test.yaml and .module.yaml files, checked by running the changed steps

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: a project set up with Momentic, its CLI and its MCP tools

glance.label: Asks first
glance.text: before running steps that submit, buy, delete or send, editing a shared module, or running a long full test

tldr.text: Momentic is an end-to-end testing tool built on Playwright: test steps are plain-language instructions, such as clicking the "Sign up" button, that AI turns into actions in a real browser. For a known change to a test in the current v2 format, which is written to be edited by hand, it edits the YAML, lints it and runs the affected steps. For an old v1 file, which it never edits directly, an unfamiliar screen or a new flow, it opens a browser session, tries a few steps at a time up to a stable point such as "logged in", saves the ones that work into the test, and reruns them. It prefers describing elements to CSS selectors, few assertions, AI Actions for new tests (a single step that states a goal, which the agent plays out and Momentic caches for replay), and shared modules for flows of four or more steps. It avoids fixed sleeps, clicking through browser JavaScript, and weakening a test to hide a broken app. After about three failed attempts at the same problem, it stops and asks you. Unlike general Playwright testing skills, it only applies to projects that use Momentic.

skills.name: caveman
skills.description: Switches to ultra-compressed answers that keep technical accuracy.

glance.label: Use it when

glance.text: makes the agent answer first, in short plain sentences, with no greetings, hedging or recaps

glance.label: Keeps
glance.text: code, commands, numbers, errors and every "not" exact

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: for the whole session, until you say "stop caveman"

tldr.text: Despite the name, it's a writing discipline more than a joke voice: each reply leads with the answer, then the reason, then the next step. It cuts ceremony ("Sure!", "Let me…", "Hope this helps"), filler words and invented abbreviations, and may drop articles where a sentence still reads in one pass, but never a negation or a number. It only changes chat replies: code, commits and docs are written normally, and it switches back to full sentences for security warnings, irreversible actions and questions to you. Once on, it stays on until you turn it off.

skills.name: caveman-commit
skills.description: Writes Conventional Commits messages compressed to intent only.

glance.text: writes a Conventional Commits message, like "feat(api): add GET /users/:id/profile", with a subject of 50 characters when possible

glance.label: You get
glance.text: the message in a code block to paste; it never stages, commits or amends

glance.label: Adds a body
glance.text: only to explain why, and always for breaking changes, security fixes, data migrations and reverts

glance.label: Leaves out
glance.text: "I", "we", "this commit", emoji and AI attribution, unless your project's rules ask for them

tldr.text: Caveman is a skill set whose main mode makes the agent reply in short, plain fragments to save tokens. That mode keeps commit messages in normal prose; this skill makes them terse too. The subject follows Conventional Commits, with a type such as feat, fix, refactor or docs, in the imperative ("add", not "added"), at most 50 characters when possible and never over 72, with no trailing period. A body is added only for a reason the diff doesn't show, a breaking change, migration notes or linked issues, wrapped at 72 characters and ending with references like "Closes #42". It drops whatever the diff already says, such as "this commit does X" or a file name the scope already gives. Breaking changes, security fixes, data migrations and reverts always get a body, for whoever debugs them later. It only writes the message; you run git. Say "stop caveman-commit" to get verbose messages back.

tldr.text: Caveman is a skill set whose main mode makes the agent reply in short, plain fragments to save tokens. This skill applies the same style to files the agent reads, rather than the replies it writes. You run /caveman-compress with a file path; a bundled Python script sends the file to your configured model, checks the output, has the model fix only what failed, up to twice, and leaves the original untouched if it still fails. Compression drops articles, filler, pleasantries, hedging and connecting words, uses short synonyms and fragments, and merges bullets that repeat each other. Code blocks, inline code, URLs, paths, commands, names, numbers and the markdown structure stay exact. It only compresses prose files such as .md or .txt, never code or config, and only the prose parts of mixed files. The original is saved as FILE.original.md in a caveman-compress folder in your user data directory, not next to the file, so the agent doesn't load it again.

It also explains how to set the default mode with the CAVEMAN_DEFAULT_MODE variable or ~/.config/caveman/config.json, including "manual", which starts sessions with caveman off until you type /caveman. tldr.text: Caveman is a skill set and plugin that makes agents terse to save tokens. New features, edits across three or more files, and reviews that need rationale stay in the main conversation or go to the default agents. The subagents switch to plain English for security warnings and irreversible actions.

skills.name: humanizer
skills.description: Removes signs of AI-generated writing from text.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a draft reads as if a chatbot wrote it and you want it to sound like a person

glance.label: It does
glance.text: finds 24 patterns from Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" guide and rewrites them, keeping the meaning and tone

glance.label: You get
glance.text: the rewritten text, optionally with a short list of what changed

glance.label: Also adds
glance.text: voice: opinions, varied sentence rhythm and first person where it fits, since clean but flat text also reads as AI

glance.label: Unlike anti-prose-slop
glance.text: that skill writes whole novels using an online service; this one edits text you already have, with no account needed

tldr.text: An editing pass based on a guide kept by Wikipedia editors who clean up AI-written articles. Its 24 patterns come in four groups, each with a before and after example. Content: puffed-up significance ("a pivotal moment"), name-dropping press coverage, tacked-on clauses like ", highlighting its importance", promotional words like "nestled" or "vibrant", vague "experts believe" and formulaic challenges-and-outlook sections. Language: words AI overuses such as "delve", "tapestry" and "underscore", "serves as" where "is" would do, "not just X, it's Y", forced groups of three and cycling through synonyms for the same thing. Style: em dashes, mechanical bold, bolded list headers, title-case headings, emojis and curly quotes. Communication: chatbot leftovers like "I hope this helps", knowledge-cutoff disclaimers, flattery, filler, hedging and upbeat generic endings. The rewrite should read naturally aloud, vary its sentences and prefer specific details to vague claims.

skills.name: anti-prose-slop
skills.description: Drafts distinctive longform prose with the Proseify MCP instead of generic AI text.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want an agent to write a whole novel or novella that doesn't read like generic AI prose

glance.label: It does
glance.text: uses Proseify, an online book-writing service for agents, to pick a genre guide, study classic passages, plan the book and draft every chapter

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a full manuscript, assembled chapter by chapter in one Markdown file

glance.label: Needs

glance.label: Unlike humanizer
glance.text: that skill cleans up existing text; this one writes long fiction from scratch

tldr.text: Despite the name, it's a whole-book writing workflow. Its one rule is "genre before prose": a gothic ghost story and a Regency romance want different sentence lengths, moods and endings, so the agent first fetches Proseify's guide to the genre: its pacing, how much dialogue it uses and the style it expects. It asks you one question up front, novel (about 80,000 words in 40 chapters) or novella (the default, 30 chapters, about 48,000 words), then searches Proseify's collection of public-domain books, mainly from Project Gutenberg, for passages in the voice it wants, and plans the book. It drafts every chapter in order at full length, because summarizing the later chapters is the usual way agents fake a finished book. Between drafts it edits out "seemed to" and "began to", stacked adverbs, "she felt" and "she noticed", repeated sentences and chapters that all open the same way. Finally Proseify scores the book and flags thin chapters, and the agent rewrites the weakest.

It then drafts two or three possible openings from the notes; you pick one, and it writes just that section into the article file. After each section it rereads the article and offers the next possible sections, saying which new ideas each would introduce, so you steer the piece one choice at a time until it ends. Its one hard rule is that no section may lean on an idea the reader hasn't met: either an earlier section explains it, or it's settled up front as something readers bring.

glance.label: You get

glance.label: Unlike writing-beats

tldr.text: It reads your whole notes file first, whatever form it takes: a list of fragments, a wall of prose, a transcript. After agreeing with you on what readers already know, it drafts two or three openings that each imply a different angle, and makes you pick one or a mix. From then on it keeps asking what the reader needs to hear next, pulls the answer from your notes, and argues with you whether that block should be a paragraph, a list, a table, a callout or a quote. Each agreed block is appended right away, so you watch the article grow, and like writing-beats it never lets a block rely on an idea that hasn't been explained yet.

skills.name: writing-fragments

You say what you'd like to write about, and the agent keeps asking: what you noticed, what happened, what you meant by a phrase you used. Anything that might survive into the final piece goes into one Markdown file: a sharp sentence, a claim with its reason, an anecdote, a quote, a half-formed thought. It pushes hardest for one coined phrase that names your idea, since the whole piece can later hang on it. It appends without asking, rereads the file before every write so your own edits survive, and never imposes headings, an outline or an order. Structure is left to writing-beats or writing-shape.

skills.description: Walks you through co-authoring docs, proposals and specs.

glance.text: you need to write a spec, proposal, design doc, RFC or decision doc that other people will read

glance.label: It does

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a finished doc, in a Markdown file or a claude.ai artifact (a document shown beside the chat), checked by a reader without your context

glance.label: Reader testing

tldr.text: A structured workflow from Anthropic for documents others will read. It offers itself when you start one, and you can decline. First you say what the doc is, who reads it and what it should achieve, then dump everything you know in any order: background, past discussions, rejected alternatives, politics. Connected tools such as Slack or Google Drive can be read directly. The agent asks 5 to 10 numbered questions until it understands the trade-offs. Next it creates the doc with placeholder sections and fills them one at a time, starting with the most uncertain: it asks questions, brainstorms 5 to 20 things the section could include, lets you keep, cut or merge them, drafts, then refines with targeted edits rather than rewrites. You're asked to say what to change rather than edit yourself, so it learns your style. Last comes reader testing: it predicts what readers would ask and puts those questions to a Claude that has only the doc and none of the conversation, through a subagent if it can or by you in a new chat if not, then fixes whatever that reader got wrong.

A 3P update covers a team's week in three short lines, Progress, Plans and Problems, with metrics where possible, so leadership can read it in under a minute. A newsletter is about 20 to 25 short bullets for the whole company, written as "we", grouped into sections and full of links to the docs, announcements and threads that drew the most attention. An FAQ collects the questions many employees are asking and answers each in a sentence or two, flagging any that need an executive. Anything else, from incident reports to leadership updates, gets general advice: ask about audience, purpose and tone, and lead with what matters most. Where it can, the agent pulls material from Slack, email, Google Drive and calendar, favouring posts with many reactions and widely attended meetings; otherwise it asks you. The formats are Anthropic's, written down in four Markdown files in the skill; to match how your company writes, you edit those files.

Beyond search it offers live GitHub code search without indexing, grep inside published packages, a document agent that answers questions about a PDF with citations, table extraction, dependency analysis from a package.json or requirements.txt, saved notes that other agents can pick up, and a code advisor that checks your files against indexed docs. skills.name: emil-design-eng
skills.description: Applies Emil Kowalski's approach to UI polish, components and animation.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're building or reviewing UI and want its animations, buttons and popovers to feel polished, not just work

glance.label: It does
glance.text: applies design engineer Emil Kowalski's rules on whether to animate, which easing to use and how fast, plus component and gesture details

glance.label: You get
glance.text: UI code with tuned motion; a review comes as one Before / After / Why table

glance.label: Unlike review-animations
glance.text: it helps you build as well as review, and isn't limited to motion code

tldr.text: The main skill of Emil Kowalski's set, mostly about animation with some general UI advice. Before writing any animation, the agent answers four questions in order. Should this animate at all? Not for keyboard shortcuts, nor for anything people see a hundred times a day. What is it for? Which easing? Ease-out for things entering or leaving, never ease-in. How fast? Under 300ms for UI. Then it applies concrete rules: pressed buttons shrink slightly, nothing grows from zero size, popovers grow out of the button that opened them, CSS transitions beat keyframe animations for anything that can be interrupted, springs suit drags, and only transform and opacity are animated so motion stays smooth. It also covers swipe-to-dismiss, reduced-motion settings and lessons from building his widely used toast library. When it reviews UI code, it answers in a single Before / After / Why table, one row per issue.

skills.name: review-animations
skills.description: Reviews motion code against a high craft bar.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want animation or motion code checked against a strict bar before it ships

glance.label: It does
glance.text: measures every animation in the change against ten standards, defaulting to flagging problems rather than approving

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a Before / After / Why table of fixes, remaining notes ranked by impact, and a Block or Approve verdict

glance.label: Unlike emil-design-eng
glance.text: that skill helps build UI in general; this one only reviews motion code, and won't write features

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: only when you invoke it by name; the agent never starts it on its own

tldr.text: A strict reviewer built on design engineer Emil Kowalski's animation rules, where approval has to be earned. Its ten standards ask whether each animation has a reason to exist, suits how often people see it, uses responsive easing, stays under 300ms, grows out of the element that triggered it, can be interrupted, animates only transform and opacity, respects reduced-motion settings, fits the product's personality, and lets deliberate actions like hold-to-delete move slowly while the release snaps back fast. Some patterns are flagged on sight, such as "transition: all", entrances from zero size, ease-in on UI, or animation on a keyboard shortcut. Fixes follow a preferred order: first delete the animation, then shorten it, then fix the easing, and only later polish. The review cites file and line, and ends with an explicit Block or Approve.

skills.name: animation-vocabulary

tldr.text: A reverse dictionary for motion. You describe what you see or feel, and it returns the precise term. "The popover seems to grow out of the button" is an origin-aware animation; "the iOS scroll that resists and snaps back" is rubber-banding. Its glossary, written into the skill, sorts about 90 terms into 12 groups, among them entrances and exits, transitions between states, scroll, feedback, easing, springs, looping motion and performance. The agent reads for the sensation rather than keywords, quotes the glossary's definitions as written, and contrasts close pairs, such as a crossfade (one element fades out as another fades in) and a morph (one shape turns into another). When nothing fits exactly, it gives the closest term and says it's an approximation instead of inventing one. Answers stay short: the name first, more only if you ask.

skills.name: apple-design
skills.description: Brings Apple's interface and physical-motion approach to the web.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're building drags, swipes, sheets or spring animations on the web that should feel as fluid as iOS

glance.label: It does
glance.text: applies Apple's WWDC developer-conference talks, mainly on fluid interfaces, translated to CSS, Pointer Events and spring animation libraries

glance.label: You get
glance.text: gesture and animation code built on Apple's own numbers: spring settings, where a flick lands, how edges resist

glance.label: Unlike emil-design-eng
glance.text: that skill covers general UI animation; this one centers on touch gestures and physics, plus glassy surfaces, typography and Apple's design principles

tldr.text: Its core idea: an interface feels alive when motion starts from where an element is on screen, keeps the finger's speed, carries momentum forward and can be grabbed and reversed at any moment. So the agent gives feedback on press rather than release, keeps dragged elements glued to the pointer from where they were grabbed, never blocks input during a transition, and uses springs instead of fixed-duration animations for anything you can touch. When you let go of a flicked element, it works out where the element would naturally stop and snaps to the nearest resting point from there, and at edges it resists softly instead of stopping dead. Beyond motion it covers frosted-glass toolbars and sheets, syncing sound and vibration with visuals, accessibility settings for motion, transparency and contrast, letter-spacing that changes with text size, and Apple's eight design principles, such as purpose, familiarity, simplicity and craft.

glance.text: you're building or reviewing UI that works but feels slightly off

glance.text: applies 19 small rules, such as matching corner curves on nested boxes, centering icons by eye, shadows over borders, and subtle press animations

glance.label: You get

tldr.text: A checklist of the small details that, added up, make an interface feel finished. Some are exact: the outer corner radius equals the inner radius plus the padding; buttons shrink to 0.96 when pressed, never below 0.95; numbers that change use fixed-width digits so the layout doesn't jump; icons swap with a set scale, fade and blur; images get a faint 1px outline in pure black or white. Every fix is written in the project's existing styling, whether Tailwind, CSS or CSS-in-JS. tldr.text: Hallmark is a strict design rulebook for agents building web pages. Its signature is structural variety: two pages for two briefs shouldn't share the same hero, three feature cards, call to action and footer. It chooses a page shape from a catalog of 21, such as Bento Grid or Long Document, plus a nav, a footer and a theme, avoiding what it used last in this project, and shows a short preview before writing code. Every colour and font must come from a named token, every button gets eight states such as hover, loading and error, and motion respects reduced-motion settings. A single component gets its file plus a preview page showing all eight states. In an existing codebase it edits in place and asks before deleting anything. On request it locks the result into a design.md that later pages follow. study never copies pixels and won't study template-marketplace pages such as ThemeForest's.

skills.name: accessibility
skills.description: Audits and fixes accessibility against WCAG 2.2.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want a web page or app checked and fixed against WCAG 2.2, the web accessibility standard

glance.label: It does
glance.text: runs a Lighthouse audit, inspects the accessibility tree, tries the flow by keyboard, edits the code to fix what fails, then audits again

glance.label: You get
glance.text: fixed code, guided by rules and before-and-after HTML, CSS and JavaScript for each WCAG area

glance.label: Works with
glance.text: Chrome DevTools MCP if available, otherwise the Lighthouse CLI or axe

It warns that automated tools catch only some problems, so a score of 100 doesn't mean the page conforms. The rest is a reference organized by WCAG's four principles (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust), with before-and-after code: alt text, contrast ratios, keyboard access, visible focus, skip links, form labels, error messages, native elements over ARIA, live announcements. It flags what's new in WCAG 2.2: tap targets of at least 24 pixels, focus never hidden behind sticky headers, alternatives to dragging, not asking for the same information twice, logins that allow paste or passkeys. It ends with a manual checklist (screen readers, 200% zoom, reduced motion) and common issues ranked by impact.

glance.label: Use it when

tldr.text: It works in five phases. First, the agent loads the page and records a trace of a fresh load. Second, it reads Chrome's insights, such as what delays the main content (LCP), which elements make the layout jump (CLS) and which files block rendering, and rates each metric against good, needs-improvement and poor thresholds. Third, it lists network requests to find blocking scripts, missing preloads, weak caching, oversized bundles and unused preconnects. Fourth, it takes an accessibility snapshot to flag gaps such as low contrast or controls without accessible names. Fifth, when the codebase is at hand, it detects the framework and bundler and checks tree-shaking, unused CSS, polyfills and compression. It's told to verify before recommending, quantify savings, skip changes with no measurable gain, name exact fixes ("compress hero.png (450KB) to WebP") and say so when a site is already fast.

glance.label: It does
glance.text: runs liarjs, a fingerprint-testing CLI, which compares what the browser says about itself with what the network saw

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a score out of 100 (85 and up Trustworthy, under 60 Likely spoofed or bot) and each failing check with a reason

tldr.text: A browser fingerprint is what a browser reveals about itself to websites: what its graphics and audio output look like, which fonts it has, its timezone, its user agent. By default it launches a throwaway Chrome with a temporary profile, probes a blank page, then deletes the profile, so your own browser data is never read. It attaches to an already running browser only when you ask. The skill tells the agent that a low score for headless Chrome is the correct result, and that the score measures internal consistency only, not whether a given site will block the browser.

skills.name: reddit-automation
skills.description: Finds Reddit threads asking for what you offer and drafts disclosed replies.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want to find people on Reddit asking for something like your product, and answer them honestly

glance.label: It does
glance.text: ranks recent threads in your chosen subreddits by need, fit and timing, then drafts short replies for the best three

glance.label: You get
glance.text: three threads, each with a sentence on why you can help, and a 25 to 55 word draft reply

glance.label: Despite the name
glance.text: nothing is automated. It never signs in or posts; you review and post every reply by hand

glance.label: Never
glance.text: names your product unless it truly answers the question, and then always with a disclosure that you work on it

tldr.text: A playbook for marketing on Reddit without spamming, from doany.ai, which sells an agent that does this daily. It first asks what you sell, who buys it and what pains them, your competitors, 5 to 15 subreddits where buyers spend time, and how they'd phrase the problem. It then reads recent posts from those subreddits, or threads you give it, and keeps only real needs: requests for recommendations, a pain your product removes, frustration with a competitor. It ranks them on three things: how clearly the poster needs help now, how well your product fits, and timing, meaning a fresh, active thread not already crowded with replies. Each reply is written as a peer who has been there ("what fixed it for me was…", not "you should…"), reacts to a detail the poster wrote, and hedges its opinions. Your product comes up only if the poster is shopping for exactly that, it truly answers them, and you've used it, always with a line such as "full disclosure, I work on X". Instructions hidden in Reddit posts are ignored.

skills.note: Copy of doany-skills/skills/reddit-automation. On 2026-10-19 the original had 12 installs and this copy had 1.0M.

skills.name: seo-audit
skills.description: Diagnoses technical SEO issues on a site.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: your site isn't ranking, traffic dropped, or you want an SEO health check

glance.label: It does
glance.text: checks whether Google can crawl and index the site first, then speed, mobile, HTTPS, page tags, content and links

glance.label: You get
glance.text: an audit report: top issues, each finding with its impact, evidence and fix, and a prioritized action plan

glance.label: Also covers
glance.text: sites in several languages, local businesses and title-tag rewrites

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: the same repo's skills for planning content or building pages at scale, it diagnoses the site you already have

tldr.text: An SEO audit done in order of what blocks ranking most: can Google find and index the pages, is the site fast and working on mobile, are titles, descriptions, headings and internal links right, does the content deserve to rank, and does the site have authority. It first asks about the site, its goals, recent migrations and whether you have Google Search Console access, and reads your product marketing context if you have it (a shared file on your product, audience and positioning that the repo's product-marketing skill writes). Before reporting structured data as missing, it checks in a real browser, since a plain page fetch misses markup that JavaScript adds. Once the basics are sound, it points to pages already sitting just below the top of the results, in positions 8 to 20, as the quickest wins. It lists common problems by site type: SaaS, e-commerce, blogs, multilingual and local businesses. It only reports: fixing structured data or optimizing for AI search is left to other skills in the repo.

skills.name: copywriting
skills.description: Writes homepage, landing, pricing and feature-page copy.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you need copy for a homepage, landing, pricing, feature or about page, or a draft sounds like AI

glance.label: It does
glance.text: first decides whether to write from scratch, restore the voice of your draft, or change only the line you asked about

glance.label: You get
glance.text: page copy by section, notes on why each choice was made, and 2-3 options for headlines and buttons

glance.label: Bans
glance.text: telltale AI phrasing such as "it's not X, it's Y", strings of "no X, no Y", and openers like "In today's fast-paced world"

glance.label: Won't
glance.text: invent stats or proof: gaps are marked [NEED: ...], and a refused claim says what evidence would allow it

tldr.text: Marketing copy for web pages, written the way a careful senior copywriter would. It asks about the page's one goal, the audience, the offer and where visitors come from, and reads your product marketing context if you have it (a shared file on your product, audience and positioning that the repo's product-marketing skill writes). Then it says which of three cases it's in. Given a blank brief or generic copy, it builds the argument but never invents facts. Given a draft with a real voice, it keeps your words and angle and fixes what's weak. Given a point edit, it changes only that line and returns just the changed lines with a reason each. It writes the page in pieces (headline, subhead, button, each section), drafting two or three versions of each and keeping the best. Every line must pass three questions: can the reader picture it, can it be proven true or false, and could a competitor write the same sentence? Most lines stay plain, with one or two punchy moments per page, and before handing over it searches the draft for a list of banned AI patterns. For line-by-line polish of existing copy, the repo has copy-editing.

glance.label: It does
glance.text: asks up to four multiple-choice questions, picks one of ten shoot modes and generates the images on Higgsfield, a platform hosting many AI image, video and audio models

glance.label: You get
glance.text: 1 to 10 image links; carousels and ad packs share one visual style

glance.label: Needs

glance.label: Unlike higgsfield-generate
glance.text: that skill makes any media from a prompt; this one is built for product shots, using Higgsfield's photography templates

tldr.text: Works best with a photo of your product. Its ten modes are a plain studio shot, the product in a real scene, a close-up with hands or a face, a vertical Pinterest pin, a wide website banner, a social carousel, a pack of ad variants, an AI model wearing the product, a surreal floating or splash shot, and a restyle of an existing image for a new mood or season. Before generating, it asks a few questions with set options, such as how many images, what style and where they'll be used, skipping any you've already answered. It then sends a short brief, and Higgsfield turns it into the final prompt from its own photography templates; the skill warns that writing the prompt by hand gives noticeably worse images. Several variants differ in lighting, angle and palette rather than being near-copies. The reply is just the image links.

skills.name: marketing-psychology
skills.description: Applies behavioral science to marketing.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want to know why people buy, or which bias or mental model fits a pricing, conversion or retention problem

glance.label: It does
glance.text: picks the mental models that apply, explains the psychology behind each, and suggests ethical ways to use them

glance.label: Covers
glance.text: 72 models, from first-principles thinking to anchoring, loss aversion, social proof and network effects

glance.label: You get
glance.text: advice in the chat, not finished copy or pages

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: copywriting from the same repo, it recommends tactics and explains them rather than writing the words

tldr.text: A reference of mental models and behavioral science for marketing decisions, in six groups: thinking tools for strategy (inversion, the 80/20 rule, finding the one bottleneck, second-order effects), how buyers decide (we value what we own, fear change, freeze with too many options), persuasion (reciprocity, scarcity, anchoring, loss aversion, framing), pricing (prices ending in 9, when "20% off" beats "$50 off", three tiers with the middle as the target), designing for action (fewer choices decide faster; behavior needs motivation, ability and a prompt) and growth (flywheels, network effects, switching costs). Each model comes with a one-line marketing example. A quick-reference table maps common problems to models: low conversions, price objections, building trust, churn, stalled growth. It asks what behavior you want to change and what currently stops it, and insists on using tactics such as scarcity only when they're genuine.

skills.name: content-strategy
skills.description: Plans what content to create and why.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you don't know what to write about, or need a content plan for your blog or site

glance.label: It does
glance.text: mines customer, keyword and competitor research for ideas, scores each one, and decides what to make first

glance.label: You get
glance.text: 3-5 core topics to own, each with a cluster of linked articles, and a ranked list of pieces with target keyword and buyer stage

glance.label: Skips
glance.text: search articles that would add nothing the current top results don't already have

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: copywriting from the same repo, it decides what to write, not the words

tldr.text: It plans content that is searchable (answers what people already look up), shareable (creates demand and gets passed around), or both, with search as the foundation. After reading your product marketing context if you have it (a shared file on your product, audience and positioning that the repo's product-marketing skill writes) and asking about your business, customers and resources, it mines ideas from keyword exports, sales-call transcripts, surveys, Reddit and Quora, competitors' blogs and support tickets. Topics are mapped to buyer stages, from "what is" through "vs" and "pricing" to "how to use". Each idea is scored on customer impact (40%), fit with your product (30%), search potential (20%) and effort (10%). It suggests a calendar of 60% searchable, 30% shareable and 10% experimental pieces, and plans distribution: one strong piece reused across channels, moving readers from other people's audiences and social platforms toward your own email list and blog.

skills.name: programmatic-seo
skills.description: Plans template-driven SEO pages at scale.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want many similar pages for search, such as "[service] in [city]", "X vs Y" or integration pages

glance.label: It does
glance.text: picks the page type that fits your data, checks there's search demand, and designs a template that gives every page unique value

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a plan, not the pages: a strategy document and a page template with URL pattern, title and description patterns, and content outline

glance.label: Guards against
glance.text: pages that only swap a city name, several pages chasing one keyword, pages nothing links to, and pages nobody searches for

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: seo-audit from the same repo, it plans new pages instead of diagnosing existing ones

tldr.text: Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from one template and a dataset, each aimed at a variation of the same search, like "crm for real estate" or "slack asana integration". The skill picks from 12 such page types: templates, best-of lists, unit conversions, comparisons, examples, locations, personas, integrations, glossaries, translations, directories and profiles, which can be combined ("best coworking spaces in San Diego"). It then works through the keyword pattern and its search volume, where the data comes from (your own data beats public data anyone can copy), the template, a category page linking to each generated page, which thin pages to keep out of Google, and whether your CMS can hold and render the pages on your main domain. Its rule is that 100 great pages beat 10,000 thin ones. A pre-launch checklist covers unique value, titles, structured data, sitemaps and crawlability, followed by what to watch after launch.

skills.name: amazon-product-research
skills.description: Analyzes demand, competition and profit for Amazon sellers.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're deciding whether a product is worth selling on Amazon, or comparing a few candidates

glance.label: It does
glance.text: searches the public web for demand, competition, prices and supplier costs, then scores the product from 1 to 10

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a report with the score, a profit breakdown, entry costs, risks and a recommendation to pursue or avoid

glance.label: Limits
glance.text: it works from public web data, so sales and costs are estimates; for live data it points to its maker Nexscope's paid analytics

glance.label: Covers
glance.text: 12 Amazon marketplaces, including the US, UK, Germany, Japan, India and Brazil

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: cross-border-ecommerce, also by Nexscope, which scores countries to expand into rather than products to sell

tldr.text: A research framework for Amazon sellers from Nexscope, an e-commerce analytics company. Given a product idea, such as yoga mats or a $3 AliExpress find selling for $25 on Amazon, the agent runs web searches in five steps: search interest and seasonality; competition, meaning how many sellers there are, which brands dominate and how reviews and prices spread; demand signals from Google Trends, related searches and Reddit; profit, from Alibaba wholesale prices and Amazon's selling and fulfilment fees; and barriers to entry such as startup capital, minimum order quantities and certifications. Eight factors, each scored 1 to 10 from a fixed rubric, combine into the overall score: demand counts 25%, competition and profit 20% each, entry difficulty 15%, and growth, differentiation, seasonality and risk the rest. The report covers the market, the competition, a cost-by-cost profit estimate, what entry takes, risks, and a strategy that depends on the score: go ahead, go ahead with changes, or avoid and consider alternatives. Several products can be compared in one table.

skills.name: audit-website
skills.description: Audits a site's SEO, performance, security and accessibility, then fixes the code.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want a site's SEO, performance, security, accessibility and content problems found and fixed in its code

glance.label: It does
glance.text: crawls the site with the squirrel CLI against 300+ rules, fixes the findings in batches and re-audits

glance.label: You get
glance.text: fixes in your code, before-and-after scores, and judgment calls such as broken links left for you

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: the squirrel CLI; audits are free signed out or offline, and cost credits when signed in

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: the seo-audit skill, which applies an SEO checklist by hand and ends with recommendations, it runs a crawler and edits your code

tldr.text: squirrelscan is a website auditing CLI, and this skill turns its report into a fix loop. The agent audits the live site when there is one, since only that shows true rendering, speed and redirects, starting with a quick 25-page pass, then a 100-page pass that samples each page template, or a 500-page full crawl before sign-off. It reads squirrel's compact text report made for agents, shows you the score, grade and worst issues, and lists the fixes it can make. Once you approve, it traces each finding to the template, component or content file behind it, fixes in batches, checks the project still builds, and re-audits until it reaches a target set by the starting score: under 50 aims for 75, 50 to 70 for 85, 70 to 85 for 90, above 85 for 95. Errors come first, then high-ranked warnings. It can diff against an earlier audit to prove progress or catch regressions. Installation, login, pricing and shareable reports are covered by a separate squirrelscan skill.

skills.name: cross-border-ecommerce
skills.description: Scores target markets for cross-border e-commerce.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you sell online in one country and want to know where to expand, how to get there and what it will cost

glance.label: It does
glance.text: asks one round of eight mostly multiple-choice questions, then scores countries on eight weighted factors, from market size and competition to tax rules and logistics

glance.label: You get
glance.text: an expansion plan: market scorecards, per-country tax, shipping and payment setup, landed costs, a four-phase roadmap, KPIs and a budget

glance.label: Data
glance.text: 2025 industry figures written into the skill, not live lookups; no API key

glance.label: Works with
glance.text: Amazon, Shopify, Etsy, TikTok Shop, Walmart, eBay, WooCommerce and multi-channel sellers

tldr.text: An advisor for e-commerce sellers going international, by Nexscope. From what you tell it (product, platform, monthly revenue, budget, the countries you're eyeing, or "recommend for me"), it scores candidate markets on market size, online share of retail, competition, regulation, logistics, payments, cultural distance and trademark protection, checks you're ready (profitable at home, able to handle more orders, with budget to set up), and goes deep on the top two or three. For each it covers tax registration (EU VAT and IOSS, UK VAT, US sales tax, Canadian, Australian and Japanese rules), which fulfillment fits your volume, from shipping direct to a local warehouse or Amazon FBA, the payment methods locals expect, such as iDEAL in the Netherlands or Pix in Brazil, translation and cultural pitfalls, trademarks, product certifications and privacy law. A landed-cost breakdown shows how shipping, duty, VAT and fees can shrink a domestic margin abroad. Estimates are flagged, and it tells you to confirm taxes with a local advisor. The report ends with a credit line linking to Nexscope, and the skill points to other Nexscope skills for marketing, ads and Amazon listings.

skills.name: landing-page-conversion-audit
skills.description: Audits a landing, sales or checkout page and ranks its conversion leaks by revenue impact.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: visitors reach a landing, sales, sign-up or checkout page, often from paid ads, and too few of them buy

glance.label: It does
glance.text: checks seven areas in order of revenue impact, starting with whether the page repeats the ad's promise

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a verdict and at most seven ranked fixes, each naming the element, the problem, the change, its effort and confidence

glance.label: Won't
glance.text: promise a percentage lift, or audit a page with no traffic yet

glance.label: Points to
glance.text: Autonnel, its authors' own open-source funnel builder, when a fix needs an offer after purchase or server-side sales tracking

tldr.text: It first asks for what it may conclude from: the page URL, the ad or keyword sending traffic, 14 to 30 days of visits and sales, where people drop off, and the split between phones and desktops. Whatever is missing limits what it claims. Then it works down its list: does the headline match the ad, does the first phone screen hold one promise, one button and a fast-loading image, can a stranger tell in five seconds what it is and what it costs, how many form fields and payment options there are, whether trust signals sit next to the button, what happens after purchase, and whether each sale can be traced back to its ad click. The report has fixed sections: whether the page is the problem or something before it, such as the audience or the offer; fixes to make now; changes to A/B test instead; what's fine; and what it couldn't check. With fewer than about 1,000 visits or 30 sales, it says the numbers are too small to tell a real problem from chance.

skills.name: admapix
skills.description: Fetches ad creatives, app rankings and market data from AdMapix.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you research app advertising: competitors' ad creatives, app-store rankings, download and revenue estimates, market data

glance.label: It does
glance.text: calls the AdMapix API with curl and returns its raw JSON

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: an AdMapix account and its API key in ADMAPIX_API_KEY

glance.label: Won't
glance.text: summarize, rank or build pages itself: the agent analyzes the data afterwards, and only if you ask

glance.label: Languages
glance.text: Chinese and English; setup help comes in the language you write in

tldr.text: AdMapix is an ad-intelligence service for apps; this skill is a thin client for its read API. The agent picks from over 30 endpoints: search and count ad creatives by keyword, country, channel or format; look up an app, its developer, similar apps and the SDKs it uses; pull app-store rankings (free, paid, grossing); get download and revenue estimates by date or country; and query market-level totals. It reads an endpoint's reference file before its first call, and turns plain requests (video ads, the games industry, last 30 days) into the request codes AdMapix expects. Responses come back untouched, field names and all, and download and revenue figures must be presented as third-party estimates. If the key is missing it makes no call: it shows how to sign up and set the key, and never accepts the key in chat. When AdMapix's MCP tool is installed, it searches creatives through that instead of curl.

The skill doesn't name particular marketplaces. Higgsfield keeps the marketplace rules and prompt templates on its side, so the agent never writes image prompts itself. It asks at most one confirmation question, then replies with the image links only.

skills.name: paper-context-resolver
skills.description: Fills the gaps a README leaves when reproducing a deep-learning paper's repo.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're reproducing a paper's code and the README leaves one specific question open, such as a dataset split or evaluation protocol

glance.label: It does
glance.text: looks up that one detail in the paper's primary sources: the README's paper link, the project page, arXiv or OpenReview

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a short answer with its sources, separating direct evidence from inference and noting any conflict with the README

glance.label: Not for
glance.text: summarizing a paper, finding a paper from its title alone, or overriding the README

glance.label: Usually called by
glance.text: RigorPilot's main skill, which reproduces a research repo from its README

tldr.text: A narrow, optional helper in RigorPilot, a set of skills that reproduces deep-learning research code by following its README. It comes in only after the README and repo files have been read and a concrete gap remains, such as which dataset version or split, which preprocessing, which evaluation protocol, or which checkpoint matches which model. It searches in a fixed order: the paper the README links, the official project or paper page, the arXiv or OpenReview record, and Google Scholar only to locate those. It answers that question alone, without a paper summary or guessed "best settings". When the paper and README disagree, it doesn't quietly switch to the paper: it records the conflict, says which source says what, and keeps the README as the default.

skills.name: archify
skills.description: Creates validated architecture, sequence and data-flow diagrams as interactive HTML.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want a diagram of a system, flow, database or history, from a description, Mermaid code or a real codebase

glance.label: It does
glance.text: picks the diagram type, draws it, then checks it automatically, including in a real browser, and fixes what fails

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a standalone HTML file, with dark and light themes, motion, and export to image, SVG or WebM

glance.label: Diagram types
glance.text: architecture, workflow, sequence, data flow, status changes, database tables, classes, tree, timeline, and where a request's time went

glance.label: Also makes
glance.text: one-page explainers that answer a question, conclusion first, when you ask for a page

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: Node.js

tldr.text: You describe a system, paste Mermaid code, or point it at a repo, and it picks one of ten diagram types. For a codebase it traces the behavior you asked about through the source and keeps that evidence with the diagram. Before handing over, it runs automated checks, including one in a real browser, and repairs and reruns when one fails. Mermaid is read for its meaning and redrawn in Archify's own style. Each diagram gets its own folder under .archify/ in your working directory, and the reply is a link to the HTML plus a line on how to read it. The second mode is the explainer: ask for an answer as a page, and it builds one that leads with the conclusion, then sections with tables, steps, diagrams and charts. Afterwards it offers, once, to make such pages unasked in future; if you agree, it adds a line to your agent's global instructions file, such as ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. It doesn't build dashboards.
