skills.name: repo-intake-and-plan
skills.description: Maps a deep-learning repo and plans a README-first reproduction.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're starting to reproduce a deep-learning repo and want it mapped before anything runs

glance.label: It does
glance.text: reads the README and setup files, lists the documented commands and sorts them into inference, evaluation, training or other

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a short repo summary, a command list, the smallest documented run worth trying first, and the ambiguities and risks

glance.label: Doesn't
glance.text: install anything, download data or model weights, run the commands or patch code

glance.label: Usually called by
glance.text: RigorPilot's main skill, which reproduces a research repo from its README, as its first step

tldr.text: The first step in RigorPilot, a set of skills that reproduces deep-learning research code by following its README. It reads the README and the usual project files (requirements.txt, environment.yml, pyproject.toml, setup.py, Dockerfile) and looks for clues in folders such as configs, scripts and examples. Commands are sorted by what they do: running the model on inputs (inference), scoring it on a benchmark (evaluation), training or fine-tuning it, or other steps like installing, downloading and preprocessing. It's conservative: explicit README commands win over guesses from file names, guessed categories are marked as inferred, and ambiguity is written down rather than settled by assumption. The run it recommends is the smallest one the README documents that can still be trusted, and you can steer it with a priority, such as inference first. Setup and the run itself are left to other RigorPilot skills.

skills.name: minimal-run-and-audit
skills.description: Runs a minimal reproduction and records the evidence.

glance.label: Use it when

glance.text: runs that one command, or takes output already captured, and writes standard report files about it

glance.label: Not for
glance.text: training runs, choosing what to reproduce, or setting up the environment

glance.label: Usually called by

tldr.text: The evidence step in RigorPilot, a set of skills that reproduces deep-learning research code by following its README. A run that passes shows the chosen command works, not that the paper's numbers were reproduced, and the reports keep that distinction. Each one states whether the run was full, partial, only a quick check, or blocked, names the documented command, separates facts from inferences and puts the main blocker up front. Two files guard what the result means: a scientific changelog lists anything that changed it, such as a different preprocessing step or checkpoint, and a comparability report says how far it can be compared with the README, the paper or a baseline. If repo files were edited to make the run work, PATCHES.md lists them, and no change to evaluation, preprocessing, checkpoints or metrics may be hidden.

glance.label: Use it when

glance.label: It does
glance.text: plans a conda environment from the README and repo files, and works out where checkpoints, datasets and caches should go

glance.label: You get
glance.text: setup notes, candidate conda commands, an asset list with sources, paths and status, and the risks still open

glance.label: Comes between
glance.text: RigorPilot's repo-mapping step (repo-intake-and-plan) and its first run (minimal-run-and-audit)

tldr.text: The setup step in RigorPilot, a set of skills that reproduces deep-learning research code by following its README. For the environment it trusts, in order, the README's instructions, the repo's environment files, package metadata, then careful guesses from imports. It reuses an existing environment.yml, otherwise translates the requirements into a simple conda-plus-pip setup, avoids aggressive upgrades and records version doubts. A script that comes with the skill can create the environment, or just print the commands. For assets it finds checkpoints, datasets and caches through README links, configs and code, sticks to documented sources, and records each one's source, local path and status: present, missing, downloaded, skipped or unknown. It targets Linux first and supports Windows and macOS where practical; containers, cluster schedulers and custom CUDA builds are out of scope.

skills.name: ai-research-explore
skills.description: Explores novel research candidates on top of a reproduced baseline.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you have a working baseline and want to try new research ideas on top of it, with the benchmark and evaluation fixed in advance

glance.label: It does
glance.text: ranks candidate ideas, tests them one at a time on an isolated branch, and compares each with the baseline

glance.label: You get
glance.text: results in explore_outputs, marked as candidates and never as reproduced results, with notes on what changed and how comparable they are

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: you to ask for exploration explicitly, and a saved baseline: a branch, commit, checkpoint or run record

glance.label: Unlike RigorPilot's reproduction skills
glance.text: it tries new ideas instead of rerunning what the README documents

tldr.text: The exploration side of RigorPilot, a set of skills that reproduces deep-learning research code by following its README, kept separate from its reproduction work. You fix the ground rules first: task, dataset, benchmark, how results are evaluated, the state-of-the-art results you compare against, and a compute budget. The agent then alternates between planning and trying. While planning, it studies the repo, keeps your own ideas, adds a few single-change ideas of its own, looks up supporting papers (in a local reference manager such as Zotero first, the web optionally) and ranks ideas by expected gain, cost, risk and ease of rollback. While trying, it makes one bounded change or run, checks it quickly, collects evidence and ranks it against the baseline; measured results outrank predictions. It stops for you at blockers, unclear scientific meaning, an exhausted budget or ideas too close to call. It won't call a gain new or state-of-the-art without a literature comparison, ablations and a fair comparison.

skills.description: Logs learnings, errors and corrections so the agent improves over time.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want your OpenClaw agent to remember its errors, your corrections and missing features across sessions

glance.label: It does
glance.text: logs them to Markdown files in .learnings/, then turns proven lessons into short rules in the files every session loads

glance.label: You get
glance.text: three log files and, over time, rules in AGENTS.md, TOOLS.md or SOUL.md, each linked to its source entry

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: OpenClaw, an open-source personal AI agent; the author keeps a separate version for other agents

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: by itself when a command fails or you correct it; an optional hook adds reminders

tldr.text: The agent creates .learnings/ with LEARNINGS.md (corrections, knowledge gaps, better approaches), ERRORS.md (failed commands and integrations) and FEATURE_REQUESTS.md, and adds an entry whenever a command fails, you say "no, that's not right", or you ask for something it can't do. Repeats are spotted and counted instead of logged twice. A lesson that keeps recurring or applies broadly is checked, then rewritten as a short prevention rule in one of the files OpenClaw loads into every session: workflow rules in AGENTS.md, tool gotchas in TOOLS.md, behaviour in SOUL.md, the file that holds the agent's personality and principles. Old lessons are kept honest: each one notes why it could stop being true (the facts changed, a decision was replaced, a dependency was upgraded, or it no longer applies) and is rechecked before reuse, never deleted just for being old. It avoids logging secrets and never changes skills without your approval. The optional hook adds a reminder at session start and scans finished sessions for errors.

skills.note: This version is built for OpenClaw only. The multi-agent original lives in pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills.

skills.name: self-improving
skills.description: Makes the agent review its own work and keep a self-organizing memory.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you keep correcting the agent on the same things and want lessons to stick across sessions

glance.label: It does
glance.text: logs your corrections and its own reflections after big tasks, and turns lessons repeated three times into rules

glance.label: Keeps
glance.text: a memory folder in your home directory: a short file loaded every time, files per project and topic, and an archive

glance.label: Setup
glance.text: creates that folder and adds a few lines to your agent's instruction files, without removing what's there

glance.label: Runs
glance.text: on its own, when you correct it, a command fails or it finishes significant work

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: skills that log lessons to a folder inside each project, its memory is shared across projects and sorted by how often each rule is used

tldr.text: It makes the agent learn from mistakes. Explicit corrections ("no, that's wrong", "I prefer X", "stop doing Y") go to a corrections log, and after significant work the agent notes what could have gone better. A lesson seen three times becomes a candidate rule, confirmed with you, and moves into memory.md, a file of at most 100 lines loaded before every non-trivial task. Lessons for one project or topic, such as code or writing, get their own files, loaded only when relevant. A rule unused for 30 days leaves the always-loaded file, and after 90 days goes to an archive; nothing is deleted without asking. When rules conflict, the most specific wins, and the agent cites which file a choice came from. You can ask what it has learned, export everything or have it forget something. It never stores credentials or health data and makes no network requests. Setup assumes a workspace like OpenClaw's (an open-source personal AI agent): it adds lines to AGENTS.md, SOUL.md and HEARTBEAT.md, and a periodic check keeps the memory tidy. Setup also offers a separate Proactivity skill, installed only if you agree.

skills.name: ontology
skills.description: Keeps agent memory as a typed knowledge graph.

glance.text: you want the agent to remember people, projects, tasks and events as linked records, or several skills to share that data

glance.label: It does
glance.text: stores each person, project, task or event as a typed record linked to others, in a local file, checked against rules you can set

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a knowledge graph in memory/ontology/graph.jsonl, read and edited with a bundled Python script

glance.label: Triggers on
glance.text: phrases like "remember that…", "what do I know about X?" or "link X to Y"

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: Python 3, for the bundled script

glance.label: Unlike note-based memory
glance.text: it keeps structured records with fixed fields and links, not free-text notes

tldr.text: Everything the agent remembers becomes a record with a type, fields and links: a Task that belongs to a Project owned by a Person. It ships types for people, organizations, projects, tasks, goals, events, documents, messages and accounts; passwords and tokens are never stored, only a pointer to where they're kept. In memory/ontology/schema.yaml you can set rules: required fields, allowed statuses, which types a link may join, and no circular blockers between tasks. The validate command checks those, and the skill warns that rules beyond them may be guidance only. Changes are appended rather than overwriting history. It also suggests writing a multi-step plan as a list of records to create and link, and lets other skills declare which types they read and write, so they can share the same data.

skills.name: proactive-agent
skills.description: Turns the agent into a partner that anticipates needs.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you run an always-on assistant such as OpenClaw and want it to act without being asked and not forget details

glance.label: It does
glance.text: gives it standing habits: save details to file before replying, check in on a schedule, try many fixes before asking for help

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a workspace of memory and rule files (SESSION-STATE.md, USER.md, SOUL.md, HEARTBEAT.md…), filled in through an onboarding interview

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: an agent with scheduled jobs and memory search, such as OpenClaw, an open-source personal AI agent

glance.label: Keeps
glance.text: you in charge of anything external: it drafts emails and builds tools, but doesn't send or publish without approval

tldr.text: It's a set of habits for a long-running assistant, in three groups. Proactive: the agent asks what would help you, suggests things you didn't think to ask for, follows up on decisions after a week, and offers to automate anything you've asked for three times. Persistent: it treats the conversation as something it will lose, so corrections, names, preferences, decisions and numbers go into SESSION-STATE.md before it replies; once the context is 60% full, every exchange is also logged to a buffer file, which it reads first after the conversation is summarized to free space. Self-improving: it tries five to ten approaches before saying it can't, tests a feature before calling it done, and changes its own rules only when the change would help often or prevent failures, favouring stability over novelty. It also adds security rules, such as treating emails and web pages as data, not commands, and vetting skills before installing them. Scheduled check-ins, which it calls heartbeats, run its checklists.

skills.name: is-this-photo-real
skills.description: Checks whether an image or video is authentic and correctly captioned.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a photo or video is circulating and you need to know if it's authentic, edited, AI-made or a real image with a false caption

glance.label: It does
glance.text: looks for where the image first appeared before any pixel forensics, since most deceptive media is real footage with a wrong caption

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a graded finding for each claim, such as "confirmed recontextualised" (an older real image reused with a new caption), saying what was tested and what it rests on

glance.label: Distrusts
glance.text: AI-detector scores, and forensic filters run on files a social platform has already recompressed

glance.label: Unlike find-the-original-image
glance.text: which finds where a picture was published, this decides whether it's genuine and correctly described

tldr.text: Its rule is provenance first, pixels last. The agent first pins down the claim being tested: that the image shows a given event, that it's unaltered, that someone said something on video, that it was AI-generated, or that a screenshot is genuine. It gets the least-processed copy it can, searches for earlier appearances, reads the metadata and any C2PA Content Credentials (a signed edit history some cameras and tools attach), then checks signs, weather, shadows, reflections and perspective against the claimed time and place. Forensics on the pixels themselves, such as noise, JPEG compression and cloned regions, come last, and only on files no platform has recompressed. For AI images it relies on tells grounded in physics, like impossible lighting or objects that don't connect, more than on finger counts. For video it inspects the encoder, frames, audio and the edges of faces, and reverse-searches stills from it. The write-up says what was verified and what wasn't, never a bare "fake" or "real". It also flags legal risks, such as defamation, and what you disclose by uploading media to online tools.

skills.name: investigate-without-getting-made
skills.description: Keeps an investigator's IP, browser and TLS fingerprints from giving them away.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're researching a person or company online and they mustn't find out, for due diligence, journalism or an internal investigation

glance.label: It does
glance.text: sizes precautions to who might notice, then controls what each visit gives away: logged-in accounts, network, browser fingerprint and timing

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a setup plan that fits the risk, and a grade after each action of what the target could know, from clean to attributed

glance.label: Covers
glance.text: research personas (fake accounts) kept apart from your real identity, VPN versus residential proxy versus Tor, and one virtual machine per case

glance.label: Draws the line
glance.text: fake accounts may only watch, never draw people out or get into closed groups; never log in to the target's systems or use leaked passwords

tldr.text: Investigators are rarely caught by a clever target; they're caught by platforms doing what they advertise: showing who viewed a profile, suggesting the investigator as someone the target may know, marking a story as seen. So the main risk it guards against is being logged into a real account. The agent first asks who might notice, what they would see and what it would cost, and matches the setup to that, from a normal browser for public registries to a dedicated virtual machine and a home-style connection for capable targets, warning that an over-hardened setup gets blocked and stands out. It lists what a visit leaks, from the company that owns your network to fonts, screen size, locale and working hours, and how a real phone number, recovery email, payment card or reused avatar can tie a persona to you for good. Personas are built and aged ahead of time, kept consistent, and never reused across cases. It prefers archived copies to live visits and logs every exposure with a time. It also says plainly that fake accounts break most platforms' terms, and that impersonating a real person can be a crime.

skills.name: what-leaked-about-you
skills.description: Checks data-breach exposure for an email, username, phone or name.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you're checking which data breaches an email, username, phone number or name appears in, for a self-audit, an incident or due diligence

glance.label: It does
glance.text: reads breach records as a map of the services someone signed up for, and turns usernames found there into new leads

glance.label: You get
glance.text: the breached services and new leads, each graded by how trustworthy the record and its source are, from confirmed to rejected

glance.label: Never
glance.text: logs in with, cracks or tests a leaked password; your own passwords are checked without sending them anywhere

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: API keys for the Have I Been Pwned API and for commercial breach-search services like DeHashed; HIBP's web lookup for one email is free

tldr.text: Breach data is treated as an account map rather than a password list: an email found in a gaming forum, a fitness app and a dating site gives three platforms, three sign-up dates and often three usernames to follow. The agent starts with Have I Been Pwned, the breach-lookup service that verifies and names each breach, and turns to commercial services such as DeHashed, IntelX or Snusbase when it needs actual field values or a search by username, phone or IP. Passwords you hold are checked with HIBP's password lookup, where only the first five characters of the password's hash leave your machine. It warns about the usual traps: credential lists merged from many sources that no longer say where a record came from, old or invented breaches sold as new, scraped public profiles labelled as hacks, and email addresses that were reassigned. If two identities share one unusual password, that's noted as a likely link between them, with the password redacted. It never uses a leaked credential or tries a password reset, and it covers the data-protection rules for holding breach data.

skills.name: find-the-original-image
skills.description: Finds where a picture first appeared with reverse image search.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you need to know where a picture came from: a profile photo, a viral image, a product shot or a frame of a video

glance.label: It does
glance.text: reverse-searches it on Yandex, Google Lens, Bing, TinEye and Baidu, crops and mirrors it to search again, then reads the earliest pages found

glance.label: You get
glance.text: the earliest known copy, with its photographer, caption and date, graded from "confirmed original source" down to "unconfirmed"

glance.label: Unlike is-this-photo-real
glance.text: it finds where an image was published, not whether its pixels were edited or generated

glance.label: Face search
glance.text: engines like PimEyes only with written authorization or a protective purpose, such as a fraud case or checking your own face, never to name a stranger

tldr.text: The goal isn't a match but the earliest publication, because that page names the photographer, the date and the caption. The agent picks engines by what the picture shows: Yandex for faces and for places outside North America and Western Europe, Google Lens for products, landmarks and text in the image, Bing for searching one region of a cluttered photo, TinEye for sorting copies oldest first, Baidu for Chinese content. It runs at least three, then crops to one unusual detail such as a sign, logo or tattoo, mirrors the image, and searches each version again. For video it searches stills taken from it. It opens every hit to collect credits, captions, dates and file names, and checks a page's date against web archives. No results counts as no evidence either way, and a headshot found on many unrelated sites is flagged as a stock photo, often the sign of a fake profile. It archives each hit before it disappears, and sends suspected fakes on to is-this-photo-real.

skills.name: multi-account-isolation
skills.description: Verifies that browser profiles are actually isolated from each other.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you run several of your own accounts or test identities on one machine and want proof their browsers are kept apart

glance.label: It does
glance.text: checks each profile: its clock matches its proxy's country, its real IP doesn't leak, and no two profiles share a fingerprint, address or cookies

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a pass or fail on 11 checks, an order for tracking down failures, and the three checks worth automating in CI

glance.label: Works with
glance.text: profiles made with the anti-detect-browser SDK, plus public test sites such as CreepJS and browserleaks

glance.label: Unlike anti-detect-browser
glance.text: that SDK creates the profiles; this verifies them, and lists what no browser setting can hide

tldr.text: A checklist for proving, not assuming, that browser profiles share nothing. Its rule is one of everything per identity: one profile, one fingerprint (the device details a site reads to recognize a browser), one proxy, one timezone. Each profile runs through its own proxy and is checked by assertion, not by eye. Its 11 checks include: does the clock match the proxy's country, does the real IP leak past the proxy, does the fingerprint stay identical after a relaunch, and do any two profiles share an address, a fingerprint or a cookie folder. When something fails, it works from the cheapest cause up: a reused profile name, a shared IP, a wrong clock, and only then the fingerprint. Since antibrow's browser is closed-source, it also shows how to watch what it sends out, through a proxy whose logs you can read. And it says what isolation can't cover: a shared card or phone number, identical activity, ID checks, a platform's own decision. A clean result means only that the browser isn't the problem. It's meant for identities you own or are authorized to run.

skills.name: playwright-stealth-verify
skills.description: Checks whether an automated browser presents a coherent fingerprint.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want to measure whether your Playwright or Puppeteer browser looks like a normal one, or what a stealth plugin really changes

glance.label: It does
glance.text: runs the liarjs fingerprint check on a page your test already has, so your real launch flags, plugins and proxy are measured

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a score and list of checks to assert on in a test, such as score at least 85 or no critical failures

glance.label: Catches
glance.text: the webdriver flag left on, "HeadlessChrome" in the user agent, and overrides that miss Web Workers or don't look built-in

glance.label: Only measures
glance.text: it doesn't change the browser or try to make it look more normal

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: browser-fingerprint-audit, which scans a fresh browser from the command line, it checks your own setup from inside the test suite

tldr.text: This skill has the agent install liarjs, a fingerprint-testing library, as a dev dependency and run its check on a Playwright or Puppeteer page you already have, so the setup being measured is the one you actually run: driver, launch flags, plugins, proxy. The result holds a score and every check, so a test can require a minimum score or zero critical failures. It explains the checks that trip up automated browsers most: the automation flag the driver leaves set, a HeadlessChrome token in the user agent, a window with no browser toolbar, an override applied to the page but not to its Web Workers, and replaced functions that no longer look like built-in code. A browser started outside the tests, such as a locally patched Chromium, can be scanned too, after you confirm which one. Unless run offline, the browser fetches one liarjs.dev endpoint to learn what the network saw, and you can host that endpoint yourself. Reading a full report and failing a build are left to the sibling skills for those jobs.

skills.name: fingerprint-ci-gate
skills.description: Fails a build when a browser fingerprint regresses.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: you want CI to fail when a change to a Chromium build or browser automation makes its fingerprint less consistent

glance.label: It does
glance.text: adds a liarjs scan to the pipeline that fails below a minimum score, and compares each run with a saved known-good scan

glance.label: You get
glance.text: a CI step, a committed baseline.json, and each run's scan kept as a build artifact

glance.label: Prefers
glance.text: the comparison where some checks always fail, such as a cloud runner whose IP location never matches the browser's timezone

glance.label: Needs
glance.text: Node 22 or newer and a Chromium in the CI image

glance.label: Works with
glance.text: GitHub Actions in the skill itself; GitLab CI, Docker and a Playwright assertion in a reference file

tldr.text: liarjs is a CLI that scores how consistent a browser's fingerprint is, the details a browser reveals that sites use to spot bots. A change that makes it less consistent usually shows up weeks later, when sites start challenging or blocking the browser. This skill turns it into a failing check in a pull request, with two mechanisms. A minimum score, such as 60, fails the job below it. A baseline comparison checks the new scan against a known-good one and prints only the checks whose status changed, so it still works where some checks can never pass. The skill gives a GitHub Actions example and its rules: pin the liarjs version, since its checks change with Chrome releases; take the baseline in the same headless or headed mode the job runs in; commit baseline.json and refresh it in its own commit with the diff in the message; keep each scan as an artifact so a failure can be diagnosed later. Running offline sends nothing out of the runner but skips the 8 checks that compare the browser with the network.

skills.name: fingerprint-failure-triage
skills.description: Attributes each failing fingerprint check to the component behind it.

glance.label: Use it when
glance.text: a liarjs fingerprint scan came back with a low score, or a check such as worker-consistency or tz needs explaining

glance.label: Unlike
glance.text: browser-fingerprint-audit, which runs a scan, it interprets one

tldr.text: liarjs is a CLI that scores how consistent a browser's fingerprint is. Its score is a summary; the failing checks are the actual findings. This skill has the agent rerun the scan with passing checks included and saved as JSON, then trace each failure to one of four sources: the launch configuration (driver, flags, build), code that changes values inside the page (where it's injected matters), the network path (outgoing IP and headers), or the base system image (fonts, GPU, display). Failures that share a cause are reported as one finding. Expected failures, such as headless checks on a headless run or a timezone that doesn't match a datacenter IP, are marked so nobody investigates them. It has you change one thing at a time and compare before-and-after scans, since several checks move together. It also explains single checks, such as why worker-consistency fails when an override reached the page but not its Web Workers. An improved result is reported as "these contradictions are gone", never as a prediction of how a site will treat the browser.

tldr.text: A small skill built on two free weather services. wttr.in is the main one: a single curl call returns a one-line summary, a custom line built from codes for condition, temperature, humidity, wind and moon phase, or a full forecast. It takes city names or airport codes, metric or US units, today only or current conditions only, and can save the forecast as a PNG image. Open-Meteo is the fallback for programmatic use: the agent finds the city's coordinates, then gets JSON with temperature, wind speed and a weather code.
